studyUnit: Study Unit 3: A.1. The Statement of Comprehensive Income

question: Among the following items, which would cause the Comprehensive Income amount reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income?

options.A: Gains and losses on a fair value hedge.
options.B: Unrealized gains on trading securities.
options.C: Transition pension assets that are not recognized immediately as a component of net periodic benefit cost.
options.D: Introducing an initial public offering in the market.

correctExplanation: Comprehensive Income is the change in equity during a period from transactions and other events except for those resulting from transactions made with the owners of the company such as distribution of dividends or the sale or repurchase of shares. It includes everything on the Income Statement plus some specific items that do not appear on the Income Statement that are called “Other Comprehensive Income.” Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income Thus, only items included in Other Comprehensive Income will cause Comprehensive Income reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income. Transition pension assets or obligations that are not recognized immediately as a component of net periodic benefit cost are items that are included as Other Comprehensive Income, so they will cause Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income.

explanations.A: Comprehensive Income is the change in equity during a period from transactions and other events except for those resulting from transactions made with the owners of the company such as distribution of dividends or the sale or repurchase of shares. It includes everything on the Income Statement plus some specific items that do not appear on the Income Statement that are called “Other Comprehensive Income.” Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income Thus, only items included as Other Comprehensive Income will cause Comprehensive Income reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income. In a fair value hedge, when the relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument is highly effective, gains and losses on the derivative and the hedged item are both recognized currently in Net Income. Since gains and losses on a fair value hedge are recognized in Net Income and also in Comprehensive Income, they will not cause a difference between Comprehensive Income and Net Income. Only gains and losses on derivative instruments that are designated as, and qualify as, cash flow hedges will create a difference between Net Income and Comprehensive Income, because gains and losses on cash flow hedges are reported as Other Comprehensive Income.
explanations.B: Comprehensive Income is the change in equity during a period from transactions and other events except for those resulting from transactions made with the owners of the company such as distribution of dividends or the sale or repurchase of shares. It includes everything on the Income Statement plus some specific items that do not appear on the Income Statement that are called “Other Comprehensive Income.” Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income Thus, only items included as Other Comprehensive Income will cause Comprehensive Income reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income. Unrealized gains on trading securities are reported in Net Income, so they are also included in Comprehensive Income. Thus, they would not cause a difference between Comprehensive Income and Net Income.
explanations.D: Comprehensive Income is the change in equity during a period from transactions and other events except for those resulting from transactions made with the owners of the company such as distribution of dividends or the sale or repurchase of shares. Introducing an initial public offering in the market involves selling stock, and thus it is an owner transaction. Since it is an owner transaction, it is not part of either Comprehensive Income or Net Income, so it would not cause a difference between them.

question: Which of the following would cause the Comprehensive Income reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income?

options.B: Gains and losses of a cash flow hedge.
options.C: Dividends declared but remaining unpaid at the end of the year.

correctExplanation: Comprehensive Income is the change in equity during a period from transactions and other events except for those resulting from transactions made with the owners of the company such as distribution of dividends or the sale or repurchase of shares. It includes everything on the Income Statement plus some specific items that do not appear on the Income Statement that are called “Other Comprehensive Income.” Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income Thus, only items included in Other Comprehensive Income will cause Comprehensive Income reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income. Gains and losses of a cash flow hedge are reported in Other Comprehensive Income and not in Net Income, so they would cause Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income. Note the difference between foreign currency translation gains and losses and foreign currency remeasurement gains and losses. Foreign currency translation gains and losses are reported in Other Comprehensive Income, whereas foreign currency remeasurement gains and losses are reported in Net Income. Thus, a foreign currency remeasurement loss would be reported in Net Income and would not cause the Comprehensive Income reported in the Statement of Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income.

explanations.C: Comprehensive Income is the change in equity during a period from transactions and other events except for those resulting from transactions made with the owners of the company such as distribution of dividends or the sale or repurchase of shares. Foreign currency remeasurement gains and losses are reported in Net Income and so would also be included in Comprehensive Income, so they would not cause Comprehensive Income to differ from Net Income. studyUnit: Study Unit 3: A.1. The Statement of Comprehensive Income

question: Which of the following statements is accurate with respect to the reporting of Comprehensive Income?

options.A: Comprehensive Income Per Share must be reported.
options.B: The Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income account is a temporary account and is closed out every year.
options.C: The balance of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income is represented in the Shareholders' Equity section of the balance sheet.
options.D: Comprehensive Income must be presented as a single continuous statement including both Net Income and Other Comprehensive Income.

correctExplanation: Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income is a line in the Equity section of the balance sheet that includes the items that are not reflected on the Income Statement. Net Income flows to Retained Earnings in Equity when the year-end close is performed, so Net Income ends up in Equity. However, certain specific items are considered “Other Comprehensive Income” items, and they are not presented on the Income Statement. Instead, they go straight to Equity by means of the Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income account.

explanations.A: Comprehensive Income Per Share is not reported.
explanations.B: The word “accumulated” in “Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income” means that the balance in the account keeps accumulating. As Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income is a balance sheet account, it is a permanent account. It is never closed out, and the balance in it keeps accumulating just like any other balance sheet account. The Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income balance in the account may be referred to as AOCI. Other Comprehensive Income for a year is the amount of change in the Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income account.
explanations.D: The Statement of Comprehensive Income can be presented as a single continuous statement, including Net Income followed by Other Comprehensive Income. Or, it can be presented as two separate but consecutive financial statements: a Statement of Net Income and a Statement of Comprehensive Income presenting the components of Other Comprehensive Income. The Statement of Comprehensive Income should immediately follow the Statement of Net Income and begin with the Net Income figure.

studyUnit: Study Unit 3: A.1. The Statement of Comprehensive Income

question: A full set of financial statements presents the elements of financial statements. One of the financial statements is the statement of comprehensive income. A statement of comprehensive income will include all of the following except:

options.A: Foreign currency remeasurement losses.
options.B: Loss from discontinued operations.
options.C: Foreign currency translation adjustment.
options.D: Investments by owners.

correctExplanation: Elements of comprehensive income include revenues, expenses, gains, and losses. Comprehensive income is the change in equity (net assets) of a business entity during a period from transactions and other events and circumstances from nonowner sources. It includes all changes in equity during a period except those resulting from investments by owners and distributions to owners. Thus, comprehensive income includes all transactions that result in a change in equity except for those that result from investments by owners and distributions to owners (such as distribution of dividends or the sale or repurchase of shares). Comprehensive income includes everything on the income statement plus some specific items that do not appear on the income statement that are called “Other Comprehensive Income.” Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income Thus, investments by owners are not included in the statement of comprehensive income.

explanations.A: Elements of comprehensive income include revenues, expenses, gains, and losses. Foreign currency remeasurement losses are part of net income, and net income is a part of comprehensive income. Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income Note the difference between foreign currency remeasurement gains and losses and foreign currency translation gains and losses. Both are part of comprehensive income, but foreign currency remeasurement gains and losses are reported in net income whereas foreign currency translation gains and losses are reported in other comprehensive income.
explanations.B: Elements of comprehensive income include revenues, expenses, gains, and losses. A loss from discontinued operations is part of net income, and net income is a part of comprehensive income. Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income
explanations.C: Elements of comprehensive income include revenues, expenses, gains, and losses. A foreign currency translation adjustment is part of other comprehensive income, and other comprehensive income is a part of comprehensive income. options.B: III.

correctExplanation: The correct calculations for Net Income, Comprehensive Income and Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income are as follows: Net sales revenue $ 1,700,000 Cost of goods sold ( 750,000) Operating expenses ( 285,000) Operating income $ 665,000 Gain on sale of land 35,000 Unrealized loss on trading securities ( 23,000) Net income $ 677,000 Foreign currency translation adjustment (gain) 12,000 Unrealized loss on available-for-sale debt securities ( 31,000) Comprehensive income $ 658,000 Ending balance of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income = Opening balance + Credits during the year − Debits during the year Ending balance of Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income = $358,000 + $12,000 − $31,000 = $339,000.

explanations.A: Comprehensive Income of $677,000 is not correct because it does not include the Other Comprehensive Income items, which are the foreign currency translation adjustment and the unrealized loss on available-for-sale debt securities. $1,016,000 is not the correct ending balance of the Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income account because $1,016,000 is the total of Net Income and the ending balance of the Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income account. explanations.B: Net Income of $700,000 is incorrect because it is not reduced for the unrealized loss on trading securities. correctExplanation: Unrealized gains and losses on a debt security transferred from the held-to-maturity classification to the available-for-sale classification are reported as Other Comprehensive Income. If a held-to-maturity debt security is transferred into the available-for-sale classification, the entity must Reverse in earnings any allowance for credit losses previously recorded on the security at the transfer date Reclassify the debt security to the available-for-sale classification at its amortized cost basis (reduced by any previous writeoffs but excluding any allowance for credit losses). The amortized cost basis is used for subsequent amortization of the historical premium or discount and for comparisons of fair value and amortized cost for determining unrealized holding gains and losses going forward. Determine if an allowance for credit losses is necessary Report in Other Comprehensive Income any unrealized gain or loss on the available-for-sale debt security at the date of transfer, excluding any amount recorded in the Allowance for Credit Losses Consider whether the transfer calls into question the entity’s intent and ability to continue to classify as held-to-maturity the securities remaining in the held-to-maturity category.

explanations.D: Under U.S. GAAP, fixed assets are not written up to recognize any increase in the fair value of the asset over time. However, according to ASC 360-10-35-17, a company must write its fixed assets down if the carrying value of the assets is not recoverable and exceeds their fair value. The amount by which an impaired asset is written down is reported as a current period loss, so it is reported in earnings and not as Other Comprehensive Income.

question: Which of the following is an example of an accounting policy disclosure required in the notes to financial statements?

options.B: The company’s marketing strategy and future sales projections.
options.C: The company's long-term strategic goals and objectives.
options.D: The basis of consolidation used for preparing financial statements.

correctExplanation: For a company that consolidates its financial statements with those of other entities, the basis of consolidation is an example of an accounting policy disclosure that must be included in the notes to financial statements. It explains how a company consolidates its financial statements, detailing whether it includes subsidiaries, joint ventures, or associates in its consolidated financial statements and the methods used for consolidation.

explanations.A: Detailed salaries of executive management are not typically included in the accounting policy disclosures in the notes to financial statements. While some disclosures related to executive compensation might be required in other parts of a financial report, they are not considered accounting policies
explanations.B: Marketing strategies and sales projections are not part of accounting policy disclosures in the notes to financial statements. Accounting policy disclosures focus on the accounting principles and methods applied in financial reporting, not on business strategies or forecasts.
explanations.C: Long-term strategic goals and objectives are not part of the required accounting policy disclosures. These goals and objectives are usually found in the management discussion and analysis (MD&A) or other narrative sections of a company's annual report, not in the notes that accompany financial statements. The notes focus on accounting practices, such as revenue recognition, inventory valuation, and depreciation methods.

question: Which of the following is not a limitation of financial statements in general?

options.A: Financial statements are based on historical cost, which may not reflect current market values.
options.B: Financial statements do not include transactions of other companies, such as competitors.
options.C: Financial statements provide a qualitative assessment of management effectiveness.
options.D: Financial statements primarily reflect transactions that have already occurred.

correctExplanation: This is not a limitation of financial statements in general, because financial statements do not provide a qualitative assessment of management effectiveness. They are quantitative documents that present financial data such as assets, liabilities, income, and expenses. Any assessment of management effectiveness would come from other sources, such as management discussion and analysis (MD&A) sections or internal performance evaluations.

explanations.A: Financial statements often use historical cost as a basis for valuing assets and liabilities. This can be a limitation as historical costs may not reflect the current fair value or market value, leading to potentially outdated or irrelevant information for decision-making purposes.
explanations.B: Financial statements are specific to the reporting entity and do not provide information about other companies, including competitors. This limitation means users cannot directly compare the company’s performance with that of others solely based on its financial statements.
explanations.D: Financial statements reflect past transactions and events. They do not provide forward-looking information, which is a limitation. The historical nature of financial statements can limit their usefulness for predicting future performance or conditions.

question: A statement concerning the accounting principles employed by a company in the preparation of its publicly issued financial statements

options.A: may be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements or on the face of the income statement.
options.B: should be disclosed in the management’s discussion and analysis.
options.C: must be shown on the face of the income statement.
options.D: should be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements.

correctExplanation: Notes and supplemental information are a required part of general purpose financial reporting. “General purpose financial reporting” is defined as a full set of financial statements plus the notes to financial statements and other required supplemental information. Whenever financial statements claim to present fairly the financial position, cash flows, and results of operations in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, a description of all significant accounting policies of the company must be included. The first note to financial statements is a summary of significant accounting policies, such as what method of depreciation is being used or how inventories are valued and what cost flow assumption is being used. Disclosure of accounting policies is used to identify and describe the principles of accounting being followed by the company and the methods used for applying the principles that materially affect the presentation of the company’s financial position, cash flows, and results of operations in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles.

explanations.A: A statement concerning the accounting principles employed by a company in the preparation of its publicly issued financial statements is not disclosed on the face of the income statement. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: A statement concerning the accounting principles employed by a company in the preparation of its publicly issued financial statements is not disclosed in the Management’s Discussion and Analysis. The Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) is an important part of the financial statements that must be submitted to the SEC by all companies that report to the SEC. The purposes of the MD&A are (1) to provide a narrative explanation of the company’s financial statements for investors; (2) to improve overall financial disclosure and provide context within which the financial statements should be analyzed; and (3) to provide information about the quality and potential variability of the company’s earnings and cash flows so that investors can ascertain the likelihood that past performance is indicative of future performance. However, the MD&A section of the annual report is not the place to disclose the accounting principles employed by the company. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: A statement concerning the accounting principles employed by a company in the preparation of its publicly issued financial statements is not shown on the face of the income statement. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

options.D: Direct method of calculating net cash provided or used by operating activities.

correctExplanation: The direct method of calculating net cash provided by operating activities presents the major classes of operating cash receipts such as receipts from customers less the major classes of operating cash disbursements such as cash paid for merchandise. This presentation is different from the indirect method of presentation because the indirect method begins with net income and adjusts net income to (1) include net changes in operating cash that do not appear on the income statement and (2) to remove noncash items that are included in the income statement.

explanations.A: The cash method of determining income does not present the major classes of operating cash receipts less the major classes of operating cash disbursements.
explanations.B: The indirect method of calculating net cash provided or used by operating activities does not present the major classes of operating cash receipts less the major classes of operating cash disbursements.

question: Which one of the following should be classified as an operating activity on the statement of cash flows?

correctExplanation: Operating activities are generally part of the company's main business activities and central operations. These are essentially items that generate revenues and expenses. When accounts payable decreases, it means cash has been disbursed for operating activities. Thus a decrease in accounts payable during the year should be classified as an operating activity on the statement of cash flows.

explanations.A: The payment of a cash dividend is classified on the statement of cash flows as a financing activity, regardless of where the money to pay the dividend came from. Financing activities are the activities that a company undertakes to raise capital to finance the business, and paying a cash dividend is a financing activity.
explanations.B: The purchase of additional equipment needed for current production is classified on the statement of cash flows as an investing activity. Investing activities are those activities that the company undertakes to generate a future profit, or return, such as purchasing fixed assets.
explanations.D: An increase in cash resulting from the issuance of previously authorized common stock is classified on the statement of cash flows as a financing activity. question: The sale of available-for-sale debt securities should be accounted for on the statement of cash flows as a(n)

options.A: noncash investing and financing activity.
options.B: operating activity.
options.C: investing activity.
options.D: financing activity.

correctExplanation: Investing activities are those activities that the company undertakes to generate a future profit, or return, such as purchasing and selling fixed assets, purchasing and selling stock of other companies, purchasing and selling debt instruments, and purchasing and selling available-for-sale or held-to-maturity securities. Therefore, the sale of available-for-sale debt securities should be classified on the statement of cash flows as an investing activity. According to the FASB Accounting Standards Codification®, Paragraph 230-10-45-11, "Cash flows from purchases, sales, and maturities of available-for-sale debt securities shall be classified as cash flows from investing activities and reported gross in the statement of cash flows."

explanations.A: Noncash investing and financing activities is not a classification on the statement of cash flows but rather an item to be disclosed as a note to the statement. The sale of available-for-sale debt securities generates cash, so it would not be disclosed as a noncash transaction but instead must be classified in the body of the statement of cash flows.
explanations.B: The sale of available-for-sale debt securities is not classified on the statement of cash flows as an operating activity.
explanations.D: Financing activities are the activities that a company undertakes to raise capital to finance the business. The sale of available-for-sale debt securities is not classified on the statement of cash flows as a financing activity.

question: On November 15, 20X0, Senger Machining Corp. purchased a $300,000 U.S. Treasury bond with a maturity date of January 31, 20X1. On December 31, 20X0, Senger still owned the Treasury bond. Senger treats all highly liquid investments with maturities of three months or less when purchased as cash equivalents. On Senger’s statement of cash flows for December 31, 20X0, how should the U.S. Treasury bond be reported?

options.A: As a cash outflow from lending activities.
options.B: It should not be included.
options.C: As a part of the cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash ending balance.
options.D: As a cash outflow from investing activities.

correctExplanation: The Treasury bond with a maturity date of January 31, 20X1 was a highly liquid investment with a maturity of three months or less when it was purchased on November 15, 20X0, and therefore, it is a cash equivalent. The purchase (and sale) of a cash equivalent is not reflected on the statement of cash flows as either a cash inflow or a cash outflow. However, its balance will be included in the ending balance of cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash on the statement of cash flows.

explanations.A: The Treasury bond with a maturity date of January 31, 20X1 should not be reported as a lending activity.
explanations.B: The Treasury bond with a maturity date of January 31, 20X1 is included in the statement of cash flows.
explanations.D: The Treasury bond with a maturity date of January 31, 20X1 should not be included as an investing activity.

question: When using the statement of cash flows to evaluate a company’s continuing solvency, the most important factor to consider is the cash

explanations.D: Solvency refers to a firm's ability to cover its liabilities with its assets. Cash flows from and used for investing activities does not help a user evaluate the company's continuing solvency.

question: In preparing a statement of cash flows using the indirect method of determining cash flows from operating activities, what adjustment is needed to net income because of (1) an increase during the period in prepaid expenses and (2) the periodic amortization of premium on bonds payable?

options.A: (1) Add (2) Add
options.B: (1) Deduct (2) Add
options.C: (1) Add (2) Deduct
options.D: (1) Deduct (2) Deduct

correctExplanation: In calculating cash flows from operating activities under the indirect method, an increase in an asset account must be subtracted from net income because it represents cash paid out that is not on the income statement. Therefore, the increase in prepaid expenses will be a deduction from net income. The amortization of premium on bonds payable reduces interest expense and thus it increases net income without increasing cash. Therefore, it will also need to be deducted from net income.

explanations.A: An increase in an asset account must be deducted from net income in calculating cash flows from operating activities under the indirect method because it represents cash paid out that is not on the income statement. Therefore, the increase in prepaid expenses will be a deduction from net income. The amortization of premium on bonds payable reduces interest expense and thus it increases net income without increasing cash. Therefore, it will also need to be deducted from net income.
explanations.B: The amortization of premium on bonds payable reduces interest expense and thus it increases net income without increasing cash. Therefore, it will need to be deducted from net income in calculating cash flows from operating activities under the indirect method.
explanations.C: An increase in an asset account must be subtracted from net income because it represents cash paid out that is not on the income statement. Therefore, the increase in prepaid expenses will be a deduction from net income in calculating cash flows from operating activities under the indirect method.

question: Gray Company’s net income for 20X4 was $525,000. Depreciation expensed during the year was $56,000. Balance sheet accounts changed by the following amounts from the beginning to the end of the year: Increases: Accounts payable $152,000 Inventory $139,000 Accounts receivable (net) $78,000 Prepaid expenses $42,000 Accrued liabilities $57,000 On Gray's statement of cash flows for the year ended Decemver 31, 20X4, what amount is shown for net cash provided by operating activities?
intro: Gray Company’s net income for 20X4 was $525,000. Depreciation expensed during the year was $56,000. Balance sheet accounts changed by the following amounts from the beginning to the end of the year: Increases:
tail: On Gray's statement of cash flows for the year ended Decemver 31, 20X4, what amount is shown for net cash provided by operating activities?
correctExplanation: Using the indirect method, net cash provided by operating activities is calculated as follows: Net income $525,000 Adjustments to reconcile net income to cash provided by operating activities: Depreciation expense 56,000 Increase in accounts payable 152,000 Decrease in net accounts receivable 78,000 Decrease in prepaid expenses 42,000 Increase in inventory (139,000) Decrease in accrued liabilities (57,000) Net cash provided by operating activities $657,000

explanations.A: This answer results from adding to net income all the balance sheet operating items, both assets and liabilities, that increased during the year and deducting from net income all the balance sheet operating items that decreased during the year. Specifically, the amount of decrease in net accounts receivable and prepaid expenses are deducted from net income instead of adding them to net income; the amount of increase in inventory is added to net income instead of deducting it from net income. Whether an amount of change in an operating asset or liability account is to be added to net income or deducted from net income to calculate net cash provided by operating activities depends on whether the balance increased or decreased and whether the account is an asset or a liability. A decrease in an operating asset such as net accounts receivable or prepaid expenses increases operating cash flow and should be added to net income, not deducted from it. An increase in an operating asset account such as inventory decreases operating cash flow and should be deducted from net income, not added to it. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: This answer results from not adding depreciation back to net income to calculate the net cash provided by operating activities using the indirect method. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: This answer results from deducting from net income all the balance sheet operating items, both assets and liabilities, that increased during the year and adding to net income all the balance sheet operating items that decreased during the year. Specifically, the amount of increase in accounts payable is deducted from net income instead of adding it to net income; and the amount of decrease in accrued liabilities is added to net income instead of deducting it from net income. Whether an amount of change in an operating asset or liability account is to be added to net income or deducted from net income to calculate net cash provided by operating activities depends on whether the balance increased or decreased and whether the account is an asset or a liability. An increase in an operating liability account such as accounts payable increases operating cash flow and should be added to net income, not deducted from it. A decrease in an operating liability account such as accrued liabilities decreases operating cash flow and should be deducted from net income, not added to it. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: In a statement of cash flows (indirect method), depreciation expense should be presented as:

options.A: a deduction from net income in converting net income to net cash flows from operating activities.
options.B: an inflow of cash.

question: Which one of the following items could be identified on the cash flow statement prepared using the indirect method?

options.A: Interest expense of $200,000.
options.B: The terms of a settlement of a lawsuit that was previously accrued.
options.C: Depreciation related to buildings and equipment.
options.D: Unrealized holding gains of $50,000 on available-for-sale debt securities.

correctExplanation: The indirect method of preparing the operating activities section of the statement of cash flows starts with net income and then makes adjustments to net income to back out items that affected net income but that are either not classified as operating activities or were non-cash transactions. One of the adjustments under the indirect method is to add back the depreciation expense that is on the income statement, since depreciation is a non-cash transation. Therefore, this item would be shown on the statement of cash flows in the calculation of net cash flow from operating activities prepared according to the indirect method.

explanations.A: Interest expense (the amount of interest expense incurred, not the amount paid) would not appear separately in the presentation of net cash flow from operating activities because interest expense would be a part of the net income figure. (The actual amount of cash paid in interest is a disclosure in the statement of cash flows, but not the amount of interest expensed.)
explanations.B: The terms of a settlement of a lawsuit that was previously accrued would not appear in net cash from operating activities calculated using the indirect method in a statement of cash flows.
explanations.D: Unrealized holding gains on available-for-sale debt securities are not part of net income and they are not part of net cash from operating activities. Unrealized holding gains on AFS debt securities are recorded in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income in equity. Therefore, they would not be identified on the cash flow statement prepared using the indirect method.

As the discount is amortized, the amortization increases reported interest income and also increases the net carrying value of the asset. An increase in reported interest income also increases reported net income. question: The most commonly used method for calculating and reporting a company’s net cash flow from operating activities on its statement of cash flows is the:

options.A: Single-step method.
options.B: Multiple-step method.
options.C: Indirect method.
options.D: Direct method.

correctExplanation: The indirect method of calculating and reporting a company’s net cash flow from operating activities on its statement of cash flows is the method most commonly used.

explanations.A: "Single-step" is a method of preparing an income statement, not a method of preparing a statement of cash flows. A single-step income statement has only two groupings, revenues and expenses. Total expenses are subtracted from total revenues to determine the net income or loss. A single-step form of income statement is simpler than a multi-step income statement and eliminates potential classification problems. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: "Multiple-step" is a method of preparing an income statement, not a method of preparing a statement of cash flows. A multiple-step income statement format includes sub-classifications of income such as gross profit, operating income, income from continuing operations, and income/(loss) on discontinued operations, in addition to net income. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: The direct method is not the most commonly used method for calculating and reporting a company’s net cash flow from operating activities.

question: Below are the balances for the following accounts on the balance sheet of a company as of the end of Year 20X2 and Year 20X1. Year 20X2 Year 20X1 Cash $1,000 $ 800 Marketable securities ? 7,200 Inventory 500 500 Wages and salaries payable 2,000 2,500 Accounts payable 1,300 1,000 Accounts receivable 5,000 6,000 Prepaids 1,200 500 The marketable securities consist of money market funds, commercial paper, and U.S. Treasury Bills that all had a maturity of 3 months or less from the date they were acquired. The company has net income for Year 20X2 of $1,900, has no fixed assets, and has no investing or financing activities. Using the indirect method for preparing the cash flow statement, what is the balance in the marketable securities account as of the end of Year 20X2?
intro: Below are the balances for the following accounts on the balance sheet of a company as of the end of Year 20X2 and Year 20X1. Year 20X2 Year 20X1
tail: The marketable securities consist of money market funds, commercial paper, and U.S. Treasury Bills that all had a maturity of 3 months or less from the date they were acquired. The company has net income for Year 20X2 of $1,900, has no fixed assets, and has no investing or financing activities. Using the indirect method for preparing the cash flow statement, what is the balance in the marketable securities account as of the end of Year 20X2?
correctExplanation: In order to answer this question, it is necessary to understand three things: "Cash" on the SCF is the total of cash and cash equivalents (also restricted forms of both, though that is not needed for this question). Cash equivalents are marketable securities that had a maturity date of 3 months or less when they were acquired, and thus the marketable securities in this question are all classified as cash equivalents. The net increase (decrease) in cash and cash equivalents on the SCF during the period from all sources—operating, investing, and financing activities—must reconcile to the amount of change in the sum of cash and cash equivalents from the end of the previous period to the end of the current period. Since there were no investing or financing activities, the net cash provided by operating activities is the same as the net increase (decrease) in cash and cash equivalents from all sources. Net cash provided by operating activities is calculated as follows: Net income $ 1,900 Adjustments to reconcile net income to net cash provided by operating activities: Decrease in accounts receivable 1,000 Increase in accounts payable 300 Increase in prepaids (700) Decrease in wages and salaries payable (500) Net cash provided by operating activities $2,000 Cash and cash equivalents at the end of 20X1 were $8,000 ($800 + $7,200). Since there were no investing or financing activities, the net increase in cash and cash equivalents during the period is the same as the net cash provided by operating activities, or $2,000. Therefore, the sum of cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet at the end of 20X2 must be $10,000: $8,000 at the end of 20X1 plus $2,000 net cash provided by operating activities (which is also the net increase in cash and cash equivalents on the SCF during 20X2). question: When using the indirect method to prepare a statement of cash flows, net cash flows from operating activities are determined by adding back or deducting from net income those items included in net income that had no effect on cash. Which one of the following items should be deducted from net income when determining net cash flows from operating activities?

options.A: A decrease in accounts receivable.
options.B: A loss on the sale of plant assets.
options.C: An increase in accrued liabilities.
options.D: Amortization of a premium on a bond payable.

correctExplanation: A premium on a bond payable is an amount received over and above the bond's par value when the bond is originally issued (sold). Only the par value of the bond will be repayable as principal when the bond matures. The additional amount (the premium) received from its sale is not repaid, so it is a gain. The premium is amortized over the life of the bond as a reduction of interest expense on the bond. The amortization of the premium on a bond payable is a noncash transaction that reduces interest expense on the bond, so it increases net income. Therefore, the amount of the periodic amortization needs to be deducted from net income when determining net cash flows from operating activities using the indirect method.

explanations.A: A decrease in accounts receivable means more receivables were collected than were created during the period. The amount of the decrease should be added to net income to determine net cash flow from operating activities using the indirect method.
explanations.B: A loss on the sale of plant assets decreases net income. The loss is a part of investing activities (when combined with the book value of the assets sold to calculate the cash received from the sale) and does not belong in operating activities. Because the loss reduces net income but it is not an operating activity, the amount of the loss should be added to net income in determining net cash flows from operating activities using the indirect method. (The amount of the loss will be included in the cash inflow from the sale of the assets that will be reported in net cash flow from investing activities.)
explanations.C: An increase in accrued liabilities represents an increase in costs that have been expensed but have not yet been paid. Since net income has been reduced by those unpaid expenses, the amount of the increase in the accrued liabilities should be added to net income to determine net cash flows from operating activities using the indirect method.

question: Appalachian Outfitters Inc., a mail order supplier of camping gear, is putting together its current year Statement of Cash Flows. A comparison of the company’s year-end balance sheet to the prior year’s balance sheet shows the following changes from a year ago. Assets Cash and cash equivalents $ (600) Accounts receivable 200 Inventories (100) Gross fixed assets 4,600 Accumulated depreciation (500) Total $3,600 Accounts payable $ 250 Accruals 50 Long-term note (300) Long-term debt 1,400 Common stock 0 Retained earnings 2,200 Total $3,600 The firm’s dividend payout ratio, that is, the percentage of earnings available to common stockholders that are paid out to them as dividends, is 20%. During the current year, net cash provided by operations is
intro: Appalachian Outfitters Inc., a mail order supplier of camping gear, is putting together its current year Statement of Cash Flows. A comparison of the company’s year-end balance sheet to the prior year’s balance sheet shows the following changes from a year ago. Assets Cash and cash equivalents $ (600)
tail: The firm’s dividend payout ratio, that is, the percentage of earnings available to common stockholders that are paid out to them as dividends, is 20%. During the current year, net cash provided by operations is
correctExplanation: The first thing to do is to calculate what net income was for the period. This can be done using the dividend payout ratio of 20%, which means that 80%, of the earnings (100% − 20%) were retained by the company. If retained earnings increased by $2,200, that means that the after tax and pre-dividend income for the company is calculated as $2,200 ÷ (1 − Payout Ratio). This is $2,200 ÷ 0.8, which is equal to $2,750. Now that the company's net income is known, the net cash provided by operating activities can be calculated as follows: Net income $ 2,750 Adjustments to reconcile net income to net cash provided by operating activities: Depreciation expense 500 * Decrease in inventories 100 Increase in accounts payable 250 Increase in accruals 50 Increase in accounts receivable (200) Net cash provided by operating activities $3,450 *Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset account that carries a negative (credit) balance in the asset section of the balance sheet. The parentheses around the amount of change in accumulated depreciation in the problem indicates that the credit balance in that account increased during the year due to 500 of depreciation expense, a noncash expense, that was recorded.

explanations.A: This answer results from using the net increase in retained earnings during the year as the net income for the period. Net income increases retained earnings, but dividends paid decrease retained earnings. Dividends paid were 20% of net income, so the net increase in retained earnings ($2,200) divided by 100% − 20%, or 0.80, is the net income for the period. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: This answer results from omitting three of the adjustments needed to reconcile net income to net cash provided by operating activities: The decrease in inventories, which should be added to net income The increase in accounts payable, which should be added to net income The increase in accruals, which should be added to net income. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: This answer results from adding the decrease in cash and cash equivalents to net income in the adjustments needed to reconcile net income to net cash provided by operating activities. The amount of change in cash and cash equivalents is not a part of the calculation of net cash provided by operating activities. Instead, it is the amount to which the sum of net cash provided by operating, investing, and financing activities needs to reconcile. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: A company has purchased an asset with a 10-year useful life. It will use an accelerated depreciation method for tax purposes. For reporting purposes, it will use straight-line depreciation because this method is believed to reflect better the usage of the asset over its economic life. When applying the indirect method of calculating an entity's net operating cash flows, using financial statements prepared for tax purposes rather than accrual accounting purposes will result in

options.A: An overstatement of cash flows in the early years and then an understatement of cash flows in the later years of the economic life of depreciable assets.
options.B: An overstatement of cash flows throughout the economic life of depreciable assets.
options.C: No effect on cash flow amounts.
options.D: An understatement of cash flows throughout the economic life of depreciable assets.

correctExplanation: The amount of cash paid and received does not change because of anything reported in financial statements, whether for financial reporting purposes or on the income tax return. Cash flow is cash flow. If the net cash flow from operating activities is calculated using the financial statements, though, the numbers used to arrive at the net operating cash flow will be different from the numbers that would be used if the income tax return were used to calculate the cash flow, especially if a different method of depreciation is used for financial reporting purposes than for tax purposes. The two net incomes will be different, and the two depreciation amounts will be different. However, when the depreciation is added back to net income for each to calculate net cash from operating activities, net cash from operating activities will be exactly the same. If, for example, net income is $800,000 when $150,000 of straight-line depreciation is taken, net income will be $750,000 if $200,000 of accelerated depreciation is taken. Net cash provided by operating activities under both scenarios will be as follows (if no other adjustments to net income are needed): Straight-line Accelerated Net income 800,000 750,000 Plus: depreciation 150,000 200,000 Net cash provided by operating activities 950,000 950,000

explanations.A: The amount of cash paid and received does not change because of anything reported in financial statements, whether for financial reporting purposes or on the income tax return. Cash flow is cash flow. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

options.A: Marketing expense.
options.B: Depreciation expense.

correctExplanation: Under the indirect method, depreciation expense is added back to net income because it is a non-cash expense item that reduces net income.

question: A condensed balance sheet for Memorable Events Rentals, Inc. is below: 20X5 20X4 Cash and cash equivalents $210,000 $188,000 Accounts receivable 98,000 95,000 Property, plant, and equipment 250,000 220,000 Accumulated depreciation-PP&E (125,000) (97,000) Total assets $433,000 $406,000 Accounts payable $ 79,000 $ 89,000 Other liabilities 35,000 42,000 Bonds payable (par value) 175,000 175,000 Premium on bonds payable 4,000 5,000 Total liabilities $293,000 $311,000 Common stock $ 15,000 $ 15,000 Additional paid-in capital 65,000 65,000 Retained earnings 60,000 15,000 Total equity $140,000 $ 95,000 The company did not pay any dividends during 20X5, did not sell any equipment during the year, and purchased equipment for $30,000. Depreciation expensed was $28,000. What was the company's net cash provided by operating activities for 20X5?
intro: A condensed balance sheet for Memorable Events Rentals, Inc. is below: 20X5 20X4
tail: The company did not pay any dividends during 20X5, did not sell any equipment during the year, and purchased equipment for $30,000. Depreciation expensed was $28,000. What was the company's net cash provided by operating activities for 20X5?
correctExplanation: Net cash provided by operating activities was as follows: Net income $45,000 * Adjustments to reconcile net income to net cash provided by operating activities: Depreciation expense 28,000 Amortization of premium-bonds payable (1,000) ** Increase in accounts receivable (3,000) Decrease in accounts payable (10,000) Decrease in other liabilities (7,000) Net cash provided by operating activities $52,000 * Since no dividends were paid during 20X5, net income for 20X5 is the difference between retained earnings at the end of 20X5 and retained earnings at the end of 20X4. ** The amortization of the premium on bonds payable for 20X5 is calculated as the amount of the decrease in the credit balance in the account Premium on Bonds Payable between 20X4 and 20X5.

explanations.A: This answer results from adding the amortization of the premium on bonds payable to net income instead of deducting it from net income. When a bond is sold at a premium, the issuer receives more than the face (par) value of the bond when it is originally issued. The premium increases the initial valuation of the bond liability on the issuer’s balance sheet. The issuer amortizes the premium over the life of the bond as an adjustment to interest expense, and the amortization is a non-cash transaction. As the premium is amortized, the amortization decreases reported interest expense and decreases the net carrying value of the liability. A decrease in reported interest expense increases reported net income. Therefore, to reverse the effect of the increase to net income, the amortization of the premium should be deducted from net income when calculating net cash provided by operating activities. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: This answer results from two errors: Including the increase in property, plant, and equipment as part of (a decrease in) net cash provided by operating activities. Cash outflows for purchases and inflows for sales of equipment or any fixed asset are cash flows from investing activities, not cash flows from operating activities. Adding the amortization of the premium on bonds payable to net income instead of deducting it from net income. When a bond is sold at a premium, the issuer receives more than the face (par) value of the bond when it is originally issued. The premium increases the initial valuation of the bond liability on the issuer’s balance sheet. The issuer amortizes the premium over the life of the bond as an adjustment to interest expense, and the amortization is a non-cash transaction. As the premium is amortized, the amortization decreases reported interest expense and decreases the net carrying value of the liability. A decrease in reported interest expense increases reported net income. Therefore, to reverse the effect of the increase to net income, the amortization of the premium should be deducted from net income when calculating net cash provided by operating activities. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: This answer results from including the increase in property, plant, and equipment as part of (a decrease in) net cash provided by operating activities. question: Royce Company had the following transactions during the fiscal year ended December 31, 20X1: Accounts receivable decreased from $115,000 on December 31, 20X0 to $100,000 on December 31, 20x1. Royce's board of directors declared dividends on December 31, 20X1 of $0.05 per share on the 2.8 million shares outstanding, payable to shareholders of record on January 31, 20X2. The company did not declare or pay dividends for fiscal 20X0. Sold a truck with a net book value of $7,000 for $5,000 cash, reporting a loss of $2,000. Paid interest to bondholders of $780,000. The cash balance was $106,000 on December 31, 20X0 and $284,000 on December 31, 20X1. Royce Company uses the indirect method to prepare its 20X1 statement of cash flows. It reports a(n)

options.A: source or inflow of funds of $5,000 from the sale of the truck in the financing section.
options.B: addition of $2,000 in the operating section for the $2,000 loss on the sale of the truck.
options.C: use or outflow of funds of $140,000 in the financing section, representing dividends.
options.D: deduction of $15,000 in the operating section, representing the decrease in year-end accounts receivable.

correctExplanation: The loss on the sale of the truck requires an adjustment to net income to calculate net cash flow from operating activities under the indirect method for the statement of cash flows. explanations.A: The sale of the truck should be reported in the investing activities section of the statement of cash flows.
explanations.C: Because this cash flow did not occur in 20X1, it should not be reported in the 20X1 statement of cash flows. The dividends were paid in 20X2.

question: Royce Company had the following transactions during the fiscal year ended December 31, 20X1: Accounts receivable decreased from $115,000 on December 31, 20X0 to $100,000 on December 31, 20X1. Royce's board of directors declared dividends on December 31, 20X1 of $0.05 per share on the 2.8 million shares outstanding, payable to shareholders of record on January 31, 20X2. The company did not declare or pay dividends for fiscal 20X0. Sold a truck with a net book value of $7,000 for $5,000 cash, reporting a loss of $2,000. Paid interest to bondholders of $780,000. The cash balance was $106,000 on December 31, 20X0 and $284,000 on December 31, 20X1. The total of cash provided/used by operating activities plus cash provided/used by investing activities plus cash provided/used by financing activities is

options.A: cash provided of $178,000.
options.B: equal to net income reported for fiscal year ended December 31, 20X1.
options.C: cash used of $582,000.
options.D: cash provided of $284,000.

correctExplanation: This question is made simple by the fact that the beginning and ending cash balances are given. Since the beginning cash was $106,000 and the ending balance was $284,000, we know that the cash increased by $178,000 during the year. All transactions that involved cash will be classified as either operating, investing or financing activities, so this question is actually just asking what the change in the cash balance was during the year, which is the ending cash balance minus the beginning cash balance. The correct answer cannot be calculated using the other amounts given, because not all of the transactions that affected cash have been given. The amounts given net to a cash outflow of $760,000. Since that does not reconcile to the amount of change in the cash balance (a net cash inflow of $178,000), we know that not all the transactions that affected cash are given.

explanations.B: Net income must be adjusted for noncash items in order to determine the net change in the cash position for the period.
explanations.C: This is the decrease in accounts receivable (+$15,000) plus the proceeds from the truck sale (+$5,000) minus the interest paid to bondholders (−$780,000) plus the increase in the cash balance (+$178,000). This is incorrect because: The question asks for the total of cash provided/used by operating activities plus cash provided/used by investing activities plus cash provided/used by financing activities. All transactions that involved cash will be classified as either operating, investing or financing activities, so this question is actually just asking what the change in the cash balance was during the year. In the calculation above, the amount of change in the cash balance (ending cash balance of $284,000 − beginning cash balance of $106,000) is included as one component of the change in the cash balance, which makes no sense. The beginning and ending cash balances can be used only to calculate the net cash used or provided during the period. The amount of change in the cash balance is the number that any statement of cash flows must reconcile to. The correct answer cannot be calculated using the amounts given, because not all of the transactions that affected cash have been given. The amounts given net to a cash outflow of $760,000. Since that does not reconcile to the amount of change in the cash balance (a net cash inflow of $178,000), we know that not all the transactions that affected cash are given.
explanations.D: This is the ending cash balance.

question: An accountant is preparing the statement of cash flows using the indirect method. She found on the balance sheet that the prior year’s balance of net equipment was $295,700 and the current year’s balance of net equipment is $304,000. Depreciation expense during the current year was $22,400. During the year, the company sold equipment for $40,000, resulting in a gain of $21,600. On the statement of cash flows, what is the cash outflow for the purchase of equipment this year?
correctExplanation: The beginning balance of net fixed assets minus the current year's depreciation recorded minus the net book value of the equipment sold plus the cost of the equipment purchased equals the ending balance of net fixed assets. Beginning balance of net fixed assets = $295,700 Current year's depreciation = $22,400 Net book value of equipment sold ($40,000 sale price − $21,600 gain) = $18,400 The unknown is the cost of the equipment purchased. Therefore, letting X = the cash outflow for purchase of equipment, the formula is: $295,700 − $22,400 − $18,400 + X = $304,000 X = $49,100

explanations.B: The beginning balance of net fixed assets minus the current year's depreciation recorded minus the net book value of the equipment sold plus the cost of the equipment purchased equals the ending balance of net fixed assets. The cost of the equipment purchased is the unknown. This answer results from adding the current year depreciation instead of subtracting it. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: The beginning balance of net fixed assets minus the current year's depreciation recorded minus the net book value of the equipment sold plus the cost of the equipment purchased equals the ending balance of net fixed assets. The cost of the equipment purchased is the unknown. This answer results from subtracting the sale price of the equipment sold instead of subtracting the net book value of the equipment sold. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: The beginning balance of net fixed assets minus the current year's depreciation recorded minus the net book value of the equipment sold plus the cost of the equipment purchased equals the ending balance of net fixed assets. topic: Investing and Financing Activities, SCF Disclosures
question: Kelli Company acquired land by assuming a mortgage for the full acquisition cost. This transaction should be disclosed on Kelli’s statement of cash flows as a(n)

options.A: Financing activity.
options.B: Operating activity.
options.C: Noncash financing and investing activity.
options.D: Investing activity.

correctExplanation: The transaction should be disclosed in the statement of cash flows as a noncash financing activity and a noncash investing activity. When real estate is purchased with borrowed funds, the borrower/buyer signs the mortgage documents and the payment for the real estate is sent by the lender directly to the seller of the real estate. The cash is never recorded in the borrower’s accounts. Thus, the company acquired land, an investing activity, without any cash payment; and it became liable for a mortgage, a financing activity, without receiving any cash. Since the company did not pay or receive any cash, the two activities will not be included in the line items on the statement of cash flows. However, they must be disclosed in the statement of cash flows as noncash financing and investing activities.

explanations.A: While taking on a mortgage is a financing activity, the transaction is a noncash transaction and should be reported as a noncash financing and investing activity.
explanations.B: This is not an operating activity.
explanations.D: While acquiring land is an investing activity, the transaction is a noncash transaction and should be reported as a noncash financing and investing activity.

topic: Investing and Financing Activities, SCF Disclosures
question: An accountant is preparing a company’s cash flow statement and is evaluating how to classify certain transactions. The company paid dividends, invested in the stock of other corporations, sold plant and equipment, and reacquired some of its own stock. Which of these would be in the cash flow from financing activities in the statement of cash flow?

options.A: Only the investment in the stock of other corporations.
options.B: Only the dividends.
options.C: The dividends and the reacquiring of stock.
options.D: The selling of plant and equipment and the reacquiring of some of its stock.

correctExplanation: Financing activities are activities a company undertakes to raise capital to finance the business and the repayment of the same. Common events that are financing activities according to the Accounting Standards Codification® include the following, and the second and third items are the two items in this answer choice: Proceeds from issuance of stock. Treasury stock transactions (treasury stock is shares that have been issued and then later repurchased by the issuer.) Paying cash dividends. Proceeds from issuing debt such as bonds, mortgages, notes, and payments for debt issuance costs and repayment of principal on debt obligations. Obtaining a loan and repaying the principal of the loan. Debt prepayment or debt extinguishment costs, including call premiums paid and fees paid to lenders or third parties that are directly related to the debt prepayment or debt extinguishment, excluding accrued interest. Payments not made soon after the acquisition date of a business combination by an acquirer to settle a contingent consideration liability, up to the amount of liability recognized at the acquisition date. Payments for the settlement of the principal of zero-coupon debt instruments. A lessee classifies repayment of the principal portion (lease liability) of finance lease payments as a financing activity.

explanations.A: Investment in the stock of other corporations is a cash flow from investing activities, not a cash flow from financing activities. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: The dividends are not the only item that is classified as a cash flow from financing activities. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: The selling of plant and equipment is a cash flow from investing activities, not a cash flow from financing activities. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: In the context of integrated reporting, value creation, preservation, or erosion is

options.A: A process that optimizes or fails to optimize financial performance for the benefit of all its stakeholders.
options.B: A process that either optimizes or does not optimize financial performance for the benefit of an organization’s shareholders.
options.C: Usage of the organization’s capitals to build wealth.
options.D: The process that results in increase, decrease, or transformation of the capitals caused by the organization's business activities and outputs

correctExplanation: Value creation, preservation, or erosion is defined in the International < IR > Framework as “the process that results in increase, decrease, or transformation of the capitals caused by the organization’s business activities and outputs." The value created, preserved, or eroded for the organization is interrelated with the value it creates, preserves, or erodes for its stakeholders, and for society at large. The ability of an organization to create value for itself is dependent on the value it creates for others.

explanations.A: Value creation, preservation, or erosion is not a process that optimizes or fails to optimixze financial performance for the benefit of all its stakeholders. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: Value creation, preservation, or erosion is not a process that either optimizes or does not optimize financial performance for the benefit of an organization’s shareholders. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: Value creation, preservation, or erosion is not usage of the organization’s capitals to build wealth. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

studyUnit: Study Unit 8: A.1. Integrated Reporting

question: Integrated reporting is defined in the International < IR > Framework as

options.A: Reporting on management’s decisions with respect to corporate citizenship.
options.B: A process that results in a periodic integrated report by an organization about value creation over time.
options.C: Reporting on the organization’s use of externalities to create value.
options.D: Reporting on the social capital an organization uses in producing and providing products and services.

correctExplanation: Integrated reporting is defined in the International < IR > Framework as a process founded on integrated thinking that results in a periodic integrated report by an organization about value creation over time and related communications regarding aspects of value creation.

explanations.A: Integrated reporting is not reporting on management’s decisions with respect to corporate citizenship.
explanations.C: An externality is a positive or negative consequence of an economic activity that is received or paid for by unrelated third parties that are external to the transaction. Externalities do not create value, so integrated reporting cannot mean reporting on the organization’s use of externalities to create value.
explanations.D: Social and relationship capital is one of the "capitals," or resources, that an organization uses in producing and providing products and services, and an integrated report will include a discussion of it. However, integrated reporting involves more than reporting on an organization's social and relationship capital.

studyUnit: Study Unit 8: A.1. Integrated Reporting

question: Greener Grocers, Inc., publishes an integrated report in which the company reports on its non-financial activities. In the section of its report where it discusses its activities that benefit and improve the lives of the people in the communities where it is located, such as donating to food pantries, it is reporting on which type of capital?

options.A: Financial capital.
options.B: Natural capital.
options.C: Human capital.
options.D: Social and relationship capital.

correctExplanation: Social and relationship capital derives from the relationship between a company and the society from which it secures its license to operate. When a company reports on its activities that benefit and improve the lives of the people in the communities where it is located, it is reporting on its social and relationship capital.

explanations.A: Financial capital is the pool of funds available to an organization to use in the production of goods or the provision of services. Reporting on its activities that benefit and improve the lives of the people in the communities where it is located is not reporting on financial capital. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: Natural capital is renewable and non-renewable natural and environmental resources such as air, water, land, forests, and minerals that provide goods or services supporting the past, current, or future prosperity of an organization. Reporting on its activities that benefit and improve the lives of the people in the communities where it is located is not reporting on natural capital. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: Human capital is the skills, capabilities, and experiences of the people who work for the organization. Reporting on its activities that benefit and improve the lives of the people in the communities where it is located is not reporting on human capital. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: Which of the following is not an element of the value creation, preservation, or erosion process as communicated in an integrated report?

options.A: The organization’s external environment.
options.B: The organization’s history.
options.C: The organization’s outlook.
options.D: The organization’s business model.

correctExplanation: The organization’s history is not one of the elements of the value creation, preservation, or erosion process. The elements of the value creation process as communicated in an integrated report are inputs (the six capitals), the external environment, the organization’s mission and vision, governance, its business model, its outcomes, the transformed capitals that result from the process, and information about performance and a focus on the organization’s outlook.

explanations.A: An organization’s external environment is an element of its value creation, preservation, or erosion process. The elements of the value creation process as communicated in an integrated report are inputs (the six capitals), the external environment, the organization’s mission and vision, governance, its business model, its outcomes, the transformed capitals that result from the process, and information about performance and a focus on the organization’s outlook.
explanations.C: An organization’s outlook is an element of its value creation, preservation, or erosion process. The elements of the value creation process as communicated in an integrated report are inputs (the six capitals), the external environment, the organization’s mission and vision, governance, its business model, its outcomes, the transformed capitals that result from the process, and information about performance and a focus on the organization’s outlook.
explanations.D: An organization’s business model is an element of its value creation, preservation, or erosion process. The elements of the value creation process as communicated in an integrated report are inputs (the six capitals), the external environment, the organization’s mission and vision, governance, its business model, its outcomes, which are the transformed capitals that result from the process, and information about performance and a focus on the organization’s outlook.

studyUnit: Study Unit 8: A.1. Integrated Reporting

question: An integrated report should contain which of the following?

options.A: Competitive intelligence.
options.B: Customer demographics.
options.C: Internal usage of data and information technology.
options.D: Risks and opportunities.

correctExplanation: The risks and opportunities that affect the organization’s ability to create value over the short, medium, and long term and how is the organization dealing with them should be a part of the content of its integrated report. Other elements of an integrated report are: An organizational overview and information about the external environment: what the organization does and information about the circumstances under which it operates. The organization's governance: how the organization’s governance structure supports its ability to create value in the short, medium, and long term. Business model: an integrated report should describe the organization's business model, including key inputs, business activities, outputs, and outcomes. Strategy and resource allocation: the report should identify where the organization wants to go and how it intends to get there, including how it plans to allocate resources to implement its strategy and how it will measure achievements and outcomes for the short, medium, and long term. Performance: to what extent the organization has achieved its strategic objectives for the period, and what its outcomes are in terms of effects on the capitals. Outlook: what challenges and uncertainties the organization is likely to encounter in pursuing its strategy, and what the implications are for its business model and future performance. Basis of preparation and presentation: how the organization determines what matters to include in the integrated report, and how are those matters are quantified or evaluated.

explanations.A: Competitive intelligence is not a part of an organization’s integrated report. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: Customer demographics are not a part of an integrated report. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: An organization’s internal usage of data and information technology is not a part of an integrated report. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: Which one of the following statements regarding an integrated report is correct?

options.A: It only focuses on the creation of value over the long term.
options.B: It only contains financial information.
options.C: It must be a standalone report, separate from the company’s annual report.
options.D: It should include material matters, both positive and negative.

correctExplanation: According to the International < IR > Framework, including all material matters, both positive and negative, is one of the guiding principles for preparation and presentation of an Integrated Report. The seven principles are as follows: Strategic focus and future orientation: The report should provide information about the organization’s strategy and the way it relates to the organization’s ability to create value in the short, medium, and long term, and to its use and effects on the capitals. Connectivity of information: The report should present a holistic picture of the combination, interrelatedness, and dependencies between and among the factors that affect the organization’s ability to create value over time. Stakeholder relationships: The report should provide information about the nature and quality of the organization’s relationships with its key stakeholders and how and to what extent the organization understands, takes into account, and responds to stakeholders’ legitimate needs and interests. Materiality: The information disclosed in an integrated report should be about material matters, that is, matters that substantively affect the organization’s ability to create value over the short, medium, and long term. Conciseness: An integrated report should be concise. It should include context that is sufficient to understand the organization’s strategy, governance, performance, and prospects without including less relevant information. Reliability and completeness: The report should include all material matters, both positive and negative, in a balanced way and without material error. Consistency and comparability: The information in the report should be presented on a basis that is consistent over time, meaning reporting policies are followed consistently from one period to the next unless a change is needed to improve the quality of information reported. The information should also be presented in a way that enables comparison with other organizations to the extent it is material to the organization’s own ability to create value over time.

explanations.A: According to the International < IR > Framework, an integrated report should include insights about how the organization interacts with the external environment and the capitals to create, preserve, or erode value over the short, medium, and long term. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: An integrated report contains both financial and non-financial information. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: According to the International < IR > Framework, an integrated report should be an integral part of the annual report that may be read by all stakeholders. An organization’s stakeholders are all those who are affected by its actions and those whose actions can reasonably be expected to significantly affect the organization's creation, preservation, or erosion of value over time. They include the organization's creditors, employees, managers, owners (shareholders or business partners), customers, suppliers, local communities, government (legislators, regulators, and policymakers), non-governmental organizations, and environmental groups. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information. Accounts Receivable (16)
