question: Which of the following would be a reasonable basis for allocating the material handling costs to the units produced in an activity-based costing system (ABC)?

options.A: Number of production runs per year.
options.B: Amount of time required to produce one unit.
options.C: Number of components per completed unit.
options.D: Amount of overhead applied to each completed unit.

correctExplanation: There is a direct causal relationship between the number of components in a finished product and the amount of material handling costs incurred.

explanations.A: This allocation basis is related to batch costs and not to individual unit costs.
explanations.B: This allocation basis is the traditional basis for allocating overhead costs to the units produced when the production process is labor-intensive.
explanations.D: This is not an allocation basis but rather the result of the allocation process when determining product costs.

question: New-Rage Cosmetics has used a traditional cost accounting system to apply quality control costs uniformly to all products at a rate of 14.5% of direct labor cost. Monthly direct labor cost for Satin Sheen makeup is $27,500. In an attempt to distribute quality control costs more equitably, New-Rage is considering activity-based costing. Activity Cost Driver Cost Rates Quantity for Satin Sheen Incoming material inspection Type of material $11.50 per type 12 types In-process inspection Number of units $0.14 per unit 17,500 units Product certification Per order $77 per order 25 orders The monthly quality control cost assigned to Satin Sheen makeup using activity-based costing (ABC) is:

options.B: $88.64 per order.
options.C: $525.50 lower than the cost using the traditional system.
options.D: $525.50 higher than the cost using the traditional system.

correctExplanation: Under the traditional system, overheads are allocated based on direct labor at a rate of 14.5% of direct labor. Direct labor costs were $27,500 and 14.5% of this is $3,987.50. Under ABC we will need to make three allocations, one for each activity. For incoming materials the amount charged to Satin Sheen is $138 (12 × $11.50). For in-process inspection it is $2,450 (17,500 × $0.14). For product certification it is $1,925 (25 × $77). Adding these three amounts together, we get $4,513, which is $525.50 more than what was allocated under the traditional system.

explanations.A: This is the total of the amount that would be allocated using traditional costing and the amount that would be allocated using activity-based costing. The total of the two options has no meaning, since one or the other will be used but not both.
explanations.B: This is the total of the three cost rates: $11.50 + $0.14 + $77.00. Since all of those cost rates are for different units, totaling them is meaningless.
explanations.C: The monthly quality control cost assigned to Satin Sheen makeup using activity-based costing will be higher than the amount using the traditional system, not lower.

question: Activity-based costing (ABC) is increasingly more feasible because of technological advances that allow managers to obtain better and more timely information at relatively low cost. For this reason, a manufacturer is considering using bar-code identification for recording information on parts used by the manufacturer. A reason to use bar codes rather than other means of identification is to ensure that

options.A: Vendors use the same identification methods.
options.B: Vendors use the same part numbers.
options.C: The movement of parts is easily and quickly recorded.
options.D: The movement of all parts is recorded.

correctExplanation: Through the use of bar codes the movement and location of a product may be tracked quickly and easily without human involvement.

explanations.A: Just because a bar code system is used does not mean that vendors will use the same identification methods.
explanations.B: Just because a bar code system is used does not mean that vendors will use the same part numbers.
explanations.D: Just because the unit has a bar code on it does not mean that the bar code will be read and the movement of the unit tracked each time it is moved.

studyUnit: Study Unit 10: D.3. Activity-Based Costing

question: When using activity-based costing techniques, which one of the following departmental activities would be expected to use machine hours as a cost driver to allocate overhead costs to production?

options.A: Plant cafeteria.
options.B: Machine setups.
options.C: Material handling.
options.D: Robotics painting.

correctExplanation: Robotics uses machines to do the work of people. Machine hours (i.e., robot hours) would be an appropriate cost driver to allocate overhead costs to production.

explanations.A: In a cafeteria, the work is labor-intensive, so machine hours would not be an appropriate cost driver to use to allocate overhead to production. Direct labor hours would be more appropriate.
explanations.B: Machine setups are labor-intensive, requiring time from the plant supervisor and perhaps an engineer. Hours spent on setups by the plant supervisor and the engineer would be appropriate to use for the allocation of their salaries, which would be overhead, to production.
explanations.C: Material handling is a labor-intensive job, so machine hours would not be an appropriate cost driver. Hours spent in material handling by employees charged with that responsibility would be appropriate to use for the allocation of overhead to production.

studyUnit: Study Unit 10: D.3. Activity-Based Costing

question: A resort company allocates IT expenses to its operating departments based on the number of computers in each operating department. The majority of the IT department’s expenses are payroll. About 80% of IT’s workload is to answer phone calls from operating departments for technical support while the remaining 20% of IT’s workload is to set up new computers. The Food and Beverage operating department complains that it is being allocated more than its fair share of IT expenses. This department has recently replaced most of its computers. Those new computers do not require the same high level of technical support required by old computers in other operating departments. The best solution to this problem is to

options.A: charge IT expenses to general and administrative expenses instead of allocating.
options.B: establish a cost pool for computer setup and a cost pool for support and then allocate cost pools based on departmental usage.
options.C: change the allocation base to the number of technical support phone calls answered.
options.D: change the allocation base to time spent on answering technical support phone calls.

correctExplanation: Activity-based costing can provide the solution to this problem. Activity-based costing (ABC) is a method of allocating overhead costs to cost objects based on cost drivers, and it is not limited to allocation of manufacturing overhead. It can also be used for allocation of shared services and other costs. The cost drivers in this situation are phone calls from operating departments for technical support and setting up new computers. The company can establish a cost pool for computer setup and a cost pool for telephone support and then allocate the costs in the cost pools based on departmental usage. In activity-based costing, an activity cost pool is a group of indirect costs that are grouped together as an activity for allocation to cost objects based on a single cost allocation base. A cost object is anything that consumes an activity or activities. In this scenario, the cost objects are the user departments.

explanations.A: Charging IT expenses to general and administrative expenses instead of allocating them is not s good solution, because the company would not be able to know how its IT services are being used by the user departments. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: Using number of technical support phone calls as an allocation base would not account for the time spent on setting up new computers. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: Using time spent answering technical support phone calls as an allocation base would not account for the time spent on setting up new computers. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

studyUnit: Study Unit 10: D.3. Activity-Based Costing

question: A primary reason for a company to change from traditional costing to activity-based costing (ABC) is that ABC

options.A: is a simpler costing method to use.
options.B: eliminates indirect cost application to products.
options.C: identifies the non-value added costs of production.
options.D: reduces product undercosting or overcosting.

correctExplanation: ABC reduces product undercosting or overcosting because more allocations are performed. When compared with traditional overhead allocation, using ABC to allocate indirect costs can increase the per-unit costs of lower-volume products (which would be undercosted under traditional costing) and decrease the per-unit costs of higher-volume products (which would be overcosted under traditional costing).

explanations.A: ABC is not a simpler costing method to use. In fact, ABC is expensive and time consuming to develop, implement, and maintain Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: ABC does not eliminate indirect cost application to products. Activity-based costing is a way of allocating overhead costs to cost objects (usually products, services, or customers) based on cost drivers. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: ABC enables management to identify the activities that do not add value to the final product so those activities can be reduced or eliminated, thereby reducing costs. But ABC does not, by itself, identify the non-value added costs of production. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: All of the following are likely to be used as a cost allocation base in activity-based costing except the

options.A: number of different materials used to manufacture the product.
options.B: cost of materials used to manufacture the product.
options.C: number of vendors supplying the materials used to manufacture the product.
options.D: units of materials used to manufacture the product.

correctExplanation: Activity-based costing identifies the causal relationship between activities and the incurrence of cost, determines the underlying resource consumption cost drivers of activities, establishes cost pools related to individual resource consumption cost drivers, develops costing rates, and applies cost to product on the basis of activity consumption cost drivers. Cost allocations in ABC need to be based on activity consumption cost drivers, not on other costs. For example, a reasonable activity consumption cost driver for allocating receiving costs would be the number of purchased parts required for each product in proportion to all the purchased parts. If receiving costs were allocated according to direct material costs, then the product that had the most direct material costs would be allocated the most receiving costs. But that product would not necessarily contain the most purchased parts. It might contain only one small, very expensive purchased part. The receiving costs should be allocated among products on the basis of number of purchased direct material parts received for each product, not by the cost of the purchased parts received.

explanations.A: In activity-based costing, the number of different materials used to manufacture a product may be used as a cost allocation base to allocate the sourcing and purchasing costs as well as the receiving and material handling costs.
explanations.C: In activity-based costing, the number of vendors supplying the materials used to manufacture the product may be used as a cost allocation base to allocate the sourcing and purchasing costs.
explanations.D: In activity-based costing, the units of materials used to manufacture the product may be used as a cost allocation base to allocate the receiving costs and material handling costs.

correctExplanation: The per unit costs for direct materials and labor are simply the total budgeted costs as given divided by the number of units budgeted to be produced. Direct materials cost per unit for the ultrasound machine is $8,000 ÷ 100, or $80 per unit. Direct labor cost per unit for the ultrasound machine is $12,000 ÷ 100, or $120 per unit. Using ABC to allocate the budgeted overhead, costs in each cost pool (engineering design, material handling, and setups) will be allocated to each product and then allocated to each unit of each product. Engineering design - number of engineering changes budgeted for each product: Total budgeted usage is X-ray 2 + Ultrasound 1, for a total budgeted usage of 3. The total budgeted cost of $6,000 is divided by 3 to calculate the cost per change of $2,000. Ultrasound is budgeted for one change, so the budgeted engineering design cost for the 100 units of ultrasound machines budgeted to be manufactured is $2,000. Since 100 units are budgeted to be manufactured, the budgeted engineering design cost per unit is $2,000 ÷ 100, or $20 per unit. Material handling - number of parts budgeted to be used for each product: Total budgeted usage is X-ray 400 + Ultrasound 600, or 1,000 parts. The total cost of $5,000 is divided by 1,000 to calculate the budgeted cost per part used of $5. Ultrasound is budgeted to use 600 parts to manufacture 100 units, or 6 parts per unit. The budgeted material handling cost per unit is $5 × 6 = $30. Setup costs - number of product setups budgeted for each product: Total budgeted usage is X-ray 8 + Ultrasound 7 = 15. The total cost of $3,000 ÷ 15 = $200 per setup. Ultrasound machines are budgeted to use 7 setups, so the total setup cost allocated to all of the ultrasound production is $200 × 7, or $1,400. Since 100 units are budgeted to be manufactured, the budgeted setup cost per unit is $1,400 ÷ 100, or $14 per unit. Therefore, the total budgeted cost for one ultrasound machine is: Direct materials $ 80 Direct labor 120 Overhead: Engineering design 20 Material handling 30 Setup 14 Total $264

question: Which of the following statements about activity-based costing is not true?

question: A profitable company with five departments uses corporate-wide overhead rates for its highly diversified operation. The firm is studying a change to either allocating overhead by using departmental rates or using activity-based costing (ABC). Which one of these two methods will likely result in the use of a greater number of cost allocation bases and more accurate costing results?

options.A: ABC will result in a greater number of allocation bases; and ABC will result in more accurate costing results.
options.B: ABC will result in a greater number of allocation bases; and departmental allocation will result in more accurate costing results.

correctExplanation: Activity-based costing requires the use of a greater number of allocation bases; and activity-based costing also results in more accurate costing results. Activity-based costing focuses on individual activities as the fundamental cost objects. In ABC, the premise is that the cost of a finished product should include the cost of direct materials, direct labor and overhead costs directly attributable to that product, and it should also include a portion of the administrative costs necessary to produce the product. With ABC, the cost allocations are not based on usage of resources. Instead, they are based on activities performed and what those activities cost. ABC is much more detailed than traditional costing, because it uses many more cost pools, and each cost pool has its own cost driver. But it results in a more accurate cost for products.

question: Young Company is beginning operations, and is considering three alternative ways in which to allocate manufacturing overhead to individual units produced. Young can use a corporate-wide rate, departmental rates, or activity based costing. Young will produce many types of products in its single plant, and not all products will be processed through all departments. In which one of the following independent situations would reported net income for the first year be the same regardless of which overhead allocation method had been selected?

options.A: All ending inventory balances are zero.
options.B: The sales mix does not vary from the mix that was budgeted.
options.C: All manufacturing overhead is a fixed cost.
options.D: All production costs approach those costs that were budgeted.

correctExplanation: This is a new company just beginning operations. That fact tells us that the beginning inventory was zero. If the ending inventory is also zero, as in this answer choice, that tells us that all of the units the company produced during its first year of operation were sold during that year. Under all the ways of allocating manufacturing overhead to units produced, there would have been some variance between the actual incurred overhead and overhead allocated to production as the year passed. However, at the end of the year, the variances between the actual amount incurred and the amount of costs applied to the units produced would have been resolved, either by closing them out to COGS only or by allocating them between COGS and Ending Inventory. If ending inventory was zero, though, all of the variances would have been closed out only to COGS, regardless of which method of closing out variances the company was using. Since all production for the year was sold, 100% of actual costs incurred during the year would have been in COGS, regardless of whether a plantwide rate, a departmental rate, or activity based costing had been used. The amounts applied under each of the methods would have been different. However, when the amounts applied and the adjustments made to the COGS account to close out the variances were combined, the total amount of overhead in COGS expense would have been the same under all the methods. Sometimes it is easier to see something like this when you use numbers. So let’s say that the actual overhead incurred by Young Company during the year was $1,000,000. And let’s say that overhead applied under the various methods would have been as follows: Plantwide rate, $993,000 Departmental rates, $995,000 Activity Based Costing, $997,000 Using a plantwide rate, with total actual overhead incurred of $1,000,000, $993,000 would have been applied during production and all of that cost would have flowed to COGS because all of the production was sold. The variance between actual incurred overhead of $1,000,000 and applied overhead of $993,000, or $7,000, would have been closed out by debiting COGS for $7,000. Total overhead in COGS reported on the income statement would have been equal to the actual overhead incurred, or $1,000,000. Using departmental rates, with total actual overhead incurred of $1,000,000, $995,000 would have been applied during production and all of that cost would have flowed to COGS because all of the production was sold. The variance between actual incurred overhead of $1,000,000 and applied overhead of $995,000, or $5,000, would have been closed out by debiting COGS for $5,000. Total overhead in COGS reported on the income statement would have been equal to the actual overhead incurred, or $1,000,000. Using Activity Based Costing, with total actual overhead incurred of $1,000,000, $997,000 would have been applied during production and all of that cost would have flowed to COGS because all of the production was sold. The variance between actual incurred overhead of $1,000,000 and applied overhead of $997,000, or $3,000, would have been closed out by debiting COGS for $3,000. Total overhead in COGS reported on the income statement would have been equal to the actual overhead incurred, or $1,000,000. We can say this for certain only because all of the production was sold during the year. If some of the units produced had remained in inventory, unsold at the end of the year, the three different ways of applying the overhead to production may have resulted in three different divisions between COGS and Ending Inventory of the $1,000,000 overhead incurred during the year.

explanations.B: A sales mix that does not vary from the mix that was budgeted would not cause reported net income to be the same for the first year regardless of which overhead allocation method had been selected. See correct answer for a full explanation.
explanations.C: All manufacturing overhead being fixed would not cause reported net income to be the same for the first year regardless of which overhead allocation method had been selected. See correct answer for a full explanation.
explanations.D: Production costs that are close to those that were budgeted would not cause reported net income to be the same for the first year regardless of which overhead allocation method had been selected. See correct answer for a full explanation.

studyUnit: Study Unit 10: D.3. Activity-Based Costing

question: The use of activity-based costing normally results in

options.A: Decreased setup costs being charged to low-volume products.
options.B: Substantially lower unit costs for low-volume products than is reported by traditional product costing.
options.C: Substantially greater unit costs for low-volume products than is reported by traditional product costing.
options.D: Equalizing setup costs for all product lines.

correctExplanation: Because of the fact that ABC usually uses more allocation bases than other methods, those low-volume units that may not use much of the overall machine hours or labor hours usually end up with more overhead costs allocated to them under ABC. Traditional costing systems use things like volume (number of units produced or sold) to allocate costs. Therefore, a low-volume product would not be assigned much of the cost to be allocated. Higher-volume products would get more of the costs under traditional costing. However, number of units may not be a good indication of how much that low-volume product actually costs to produce. For example, it takes just as much time to set up a machine for a production run of 10 units as it does for a production run of 100 units. So if activity-based costing is being used and cost per setup and number of setups per product are used to allocate costs, the cost per part produced to set up the machine for a low volume product will be higher than it would be for a high volume product, because the cost will be divided over a smaller number of units for the low-volume product. ABC uses multiple cost pools (one would be as setup costs) related to multiple individual drivers (such as number of setups per product for the setup costs pool). So there will usually be several such allocations done under ABC costing. When costs are allocated by means of that method, low-volume products will usually get more costs allocated to them than under traditional costing methods, and the costs allocated to the low-volume products will be more representative of their true cost.

explanations.A: Under ABC there will probably be more setup costs charged to low volume products because the setup costs are probably allocated and distributed separately from other overhead costs.
explanations.B: Usually, under ABC the items that are low in volume have more costs charged to them than under a traditional, or other system.
explanations.D: Under ABC not all product lines will have the same setup costs because it is unlikely that every product line has the same number of setups required.

question: The costing method that determines product cost by identifying the costs of individual tasks and then assigning these costs to products on the basis of the tasks needed to produce each product is known as

options.A: process costing.
options.B: operation costing.
options.C: activity-based costing.
options.D: job order costing.

correctExplanation: Activity-based costing determines product cost by identifying the costs of individual tasks and then assigning these costs to products on the basis of the tasks needed to produce each product.

explanations.A: Process costing does not determine product cost by identifying the costs of individual tasks and then assigning these costs to products on the basis of the tasks needed to produce each product. Process costing is used to allocate costs to individual products when the products are all relatively similar and are mass-produced. Process costing is basically applicable to assembly lines and products that share a similar production process. In process costing, all of the costs incurred by a process are collected and then allocated to the individual goods that were produced, or worked on, during that period within that process. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: Operations costing does not determine product cost by identifying the costs of individual tasks and then assigning these costs to products on the basis of the tasks needed to produce each product. Operation costing is a hybrid, or combination, of job-order costing and process costing. In operating costing, a company applies the basic operation of process costing to a production process that produces batches of items. The different batches all follow a similar process, but the direct materials input to each batch are different. (Operations costing is not tested on the CMA exam.) Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: Job order costing does not determine product cost by identifying the costs of individual tasks and then assigning these costs to products on the basis of the tasks needed to produce each product. Job-order costing is a cost system in which all of the costs associated with a specific job or client are accumulated and charged to that job or client. Job-order costing can be used when all of the products or production runs are unique and identifiable from each other. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information. topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: In which one of the following situations will ending inventory on the balance sheet computed under absorption costing be exactly equal to ending inventory computed under variable costing?

options.A: When there is no fixed factory overhead cost.
options.B: When the denominator variance is zero.
options.C: When there is no variable overhead cost.
options.D: When the number of units produced equals the number of units sold.

correctExplanation: The differences between variable costing and absorption costing are (1) their treatment of fixed factory overhead costs, and (2) the income statement presentation of the different costs. In absorption costing, fixed factory overhead costs are inventoried as part of the product cost, whereas in variable costing, fixed factory overhead costs are expensed as incurred. If there is no fixed factory overhead cost, no fixed factory overhead cost can be inventoried under absorption costing. Therefore, ending inventory on the balance sheet computed under absorption costing be exactly equal to ending inventory computed under variable costing.

explanations.B: The differences between variable costing and absorption costing are (1) their treatment of fixed factory overhead costs, and (2) the income statement presentation of the different costs. In absorption costing, fixed factory overhead costs are inventoried as part of the product cost, whereas in variable costing, fixed factory overhead costs are expensed as incurred. "Denominator variance" is sometimes used as another term for the fixed overhead production-volume variance. The fixed overhead production-volume variance is Budgeted Fixed Overheads minus Standard Fixed Overhead Applied. A fixed overhead production-volume variance of zero means that actual production was exactly equal to budgeted production. Even if the production-volume variance is zero, under absorption costing fixed factory overhead would still be applied to the units produced and would be included in inventory, whereas under variable costing it would be expensed. Therefore, the ending inventory on the balance sheet computed under absorption costing would not be exactly equal to ending inventory computed under variable costing when the denominator variance (fixed overhead production-volume variance) is zero.
explanations.C: The differences between variable costing and absorption costing are (1) their treatment of fixed factory overhead costs, and (2) the income statement presentation of the different costs. In absorption costing, fixed factory overhead costs are inventoried as part of the product cost, whereas in variable costing, fixed factory overhead costs are expensed as incurred. Variable overhead costs are treated the same way under variable costing and absorption costing: they are applied to the units produced and are inventoried. Thus having no variable overhead cost would not, by itself, cause the ending inventory on the balance sheet computed under absorption costing to be exactly equal to ending inventory computed under variable costing.
explanations.D: The differences between variable costing and absorption costing are (1) their treatment of fixed factory overhead costs, and (2) the income statement presentation of the different costs. In absorption costing, fixed factory overhead costs are inventoried as part of the product cost, whereas in variable costing, fixed factory overhead costs are expensed as incurred. Whenever there are fixed factory overhead costs, ending inventory under absorption costing will always be higher than ending inventory under variable costing, because there are more costs in each unit under absorption costing, and the number of units in ending inventory are the same under both methods. There will always be some fixed costs in ending inventory under absorption costing that will not be in ending inventory under variable costing. That will be true whether the number of units produced equals the number of units sold, or whether the number of units produced is not equal to the number of units sold.

question: When comparing absorption costing with variable costing, which of the following statements is not true?

options.A: A manager who is evaluated based on variable costing operating profit would be tempted to increase production at the end of a period in order to get a more favorable review.
options.B: Absorption costing enables managers to increase operating profits in the short run by increasing inventories.
options.C: When sales volume is more than production volume, variable costing will result in higher operating profit.
options.D: Under absorption costing, operating profit is a function of both sales volume and production volume.

correctExplanation: Under variable costing, the fixed factory overheads are expensed in the period incurred, so an increase in production would not impact the income from the period, nor the manager's review.

explanations.B: This is a true statement because an increase in inventory will keep more of the fixed factory overhead on the balance sheet and off the income statement.
explanations.C: This is a true statement. When sales volume is greater than production volume, units are sold from inventory which causes the fixed cost attached to those units to reach the income statement as cost of sales under absorption costing. As a result, total fixed cost expensed would consist of all of the current year's fixed cost plus a portion of previous years' fixed costs. Under variable costing, all fixed costs would be expensed in the year incurred, so the fixed cost expensed for the current year would be only the current year's fixed cost.
explanations.D: This is a true statement. Under absorption costing, an increase in inventory will keep more of the fixed factory overhead on the balance sheet and off the income statement resulting in decreased expenses and higher operating profit. A decrease in inventory will cause some of the fixed factory overhead that is on the balance sheet to be expensed, resulting in an increase in expenses and lower operating profit.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Which of the following is an argument against the use of direct (variable) costing?

correctExplanation: Under variable, or direct, costing, fixed factory overheads are reported as period costs and are expensed in the period in which they are incurred. explanations.A: Fixed manufacturing overhead is not classified as an administrative cost under variable (or direct) costing.
explanations.C: Fixed manufacturing overhead is not classified as a selling cost under variable (or direct) costing.
explanations.D: Under variable (or direct) costing, fixed manufacturing overhead is not treated as an inventoriable cost.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Jansen, Inc. pays bonuses to its managers based on operating income. The company uses absorption costing, and overhead is applied on the basis of direct labor hours. To increase bonuses, Jansen's managers may do all of the following except

options.A: Decrease production of those items requiring the most direct labor.
options.B: Increase production schedules independent of customer demands.
options.C: Produce those products requiring the most direct labor.
options.D: Defer expenses such as maintenance to a future period.

correctExplanation: By producing fewer units that require a lot of direct labor, less of the overhead will be allocated to units that are in inventory at the end of the period because there will be fewer units in inventory. This will mean that less of the overhead is on the balance sheet and more is on the income statement, reducing net income.

explanations.B: By increasing production schedules independent of customer demand, more units will be in inventory at the end of the year, meaning that more fixed costs will be on the balance sheet and not on the income statement. This will increase income.
explanations.C: By producing more products that use a lot of direct labor, there will be more overhead included in inventory at the end of the year, since overhead is applied on the basis of direct labor hours. Since these costs are on the balance sheet instead of the income statement, income will be higher as a result of doing this.
explanations.D: By deferring expenses, the income in the current period will be higher, giving a bigger bonus.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Using absorption costing, fixed manufacturing overhead costs are best described as

options.A: Indirect period costs.
options.B: Direct period costs.
options.C: Indirect product costs.
options.D: Direct product costs.

correctExplanation: Under absorption costing fixed manufacturing overhead is allocated to the units produced and it is best classified as an indirect product cost. It is indirect because it is not directly traceable to a specific unit and a product cost because it allocated to the product.

explanations.A: Fixed manufacturing overhead is not a period cost under absorption costing because it is allocated to the units produced and not expensed.
explanations.B: Fixed manufacturing overhead is not a direct cost because it cannot be traced to a specific unit. It is also not a period cost under absorption costing because it is allocated to the units produced and not expensed.
explanations.D: Fixed manufacturing overhead is not a direct cost because it cannot be traced to a specific unit.

studyUnit: Study Unit 11: D.3. Variable and Absorption Costing

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Which one of the following is true with respect to variable and absorption costing systems?

options.A: Absorption costing systems include fixed manufacturing overhead as period costs.
options.B: Absorption costing systems include variable manufacturing overhead as period costs.
options.C: Variable costing systems include fixed manufacturing overhead as period costs.
options.D: Variable costing systems include variable manufacturing overhead as period costs.

correctExplanation: This is true. Under variable costing, fixed manufacturing overhead is accounted for as a period cost and is expensed as it is incurred.

explanations.A: This is not true. Under absorption costing, fixed manufacturing overhead is a accounted for as a product cost and is applied to production using a predetermined overhead application rate.
explanations.B: This is not true. Under absorption costing, variable manufacturing overhead is accounted for as a product cost and is applied to production using a predetermined overhead application rate.
explanations.D: This is not true. Under variable costing, variable manufacturing overhead is accounted for as a product cost and is applied to production using a predetermined overhead application rate.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: The CEO of an auto manufacturing company would like to have an impartial performance evaluation system so that managers can be fairly rewarded. Under the current costing system, managers may inflate short-run operating income by manipulating inventory levels. To meet the CEO’s expectation, the company should switch from the current

options.A: variable costing approach to the absorption costing approach.
options.B: variable costing approach to the normal costing approach.
options.C: absorption costing approach to the normal costing approach.
options.D: absorption costing approach to the variable costing approach.

correctExplanation: The company is currently using an absorption costing system for manager performance evaluation because managers are able inflate short-run operating income by manipulating inventory levels. Whenever production is greater than sales, a manufacturer's operating income calculated under absorption costing will be greater than operating income under variable costing because some of the fixed factory overheads incurred will have been capitalized in inventory under absorption costing and expensed under variable costing. Because of the way that fixed costs are allocated to units produced under absorption costing, managers can increase reported operating income by overproducing in order to keep some of the fixed costs on the balance sheet in inventory. The effect of this manipulation is to move operating income from a future period to the current period. It also creates a buildup of inventories that is not consistent with a profitable operation. Under variable costing, however, all the fixed factory overheads incurred are expensed on the income statement in the period incurred. Operating income varies directly with sales volume and is not affected by changes in inventory levels. Therefore, using variable costing for manager performance evaluation would be more impartial.

explanations.A: The company is not currently using a variable costing approach for manager performance evaluation. The company is using an absorption costing system because managers are able inflate short-run operating income by manipulating inventory levels. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: The company is not currently using a variable costing approach for manager performance evaluation. The company is using an absorption costing system because managers are able inflate short-run operating income by manipulating inventory levels. And the normal costing approach would not be an improvement for performance evaluation. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: The company is currently using an absorption costing system for manager performance evaluation because managers are able inflate short-run operating income by manipulating inventory levels, so that is correct. However, the normal costing approach would not be an improvement for performance evaluation. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Which of the following statements are true concerning the differences between variable and absorption costing? I. Under variable costing, all fixed costs are considered period costs. Under absorption costing, only non-manufacturing fixed costs are considered period costs. II. Under absorption costing, the income statement must be in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles such as U.S. GAAP. Variable costing is used for internal reporting purposes and is not in accordance with GAAP. III. Under variable costing, if production is greater than sales, operating profit will be higher than it would be under absorption costing. IV. Under absorption costing, if production is less than sales, operating profit will be higher than it would be under variable costing.

options.A: II and IV only.
options.B: I and II only.
options.C: II and III only.
options.D: I and III only.

correctExplanation: Item I is true. Under variable costing, even manufacturing fixed costs are treated as period costs. Item II is true. GAAP requires the absorption costing method. Item III is not true. If production is greater than sales, operating profit will be higher under absorption costing, not variable costing. Item IV is not true. If production is less than sales, operating profit under variable costing will be higher than it will be under absorption costing.

explanations.A: Item IV is not true. If production is less than sales, operating profit under variable costing will be higher than it will be under absorption costing.
explanations.C: Item III is not true. If production is greater than sales, operating profit will be higher under absorption costing, not variable costing.
explanations.D: Item III is not true. If production is greater than sales, operating profit will be higher under absorption costing, not variable costing.

studyUnit: Study Unit 11: D.3. Variable and Absorption Costing

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Which one of the following is the best reason for using variable costing?

options.A: Variable costing usually results in higher operating income than if a company uses absorption costing.
options.B: Variable costing is acceptable for income tax reporting purposes.
options.C: All costs are variable in the long term.
options.D: Fixed factory overhead is more closely related to the capacity to produce than to the production of specific units.

correctExplanation: The difference between net income under absorption costing and net income under variable costing is fixed manufacturing overhead. Under variable costing, all of the fixed manufacturing overhead is expensed as it is incurred. Under absorption costing, an allocated amount of fixed manufacturing overhead for the units that were sold is expensed, but an allocated amount of fixed manufacturing overhead for units manufactured but not sold remains in inventory. Variable costing separates fixed manufacturing cost from variable manufacturing cost by not including fixed manufacturing cost in the calculation of the cost to produce. The fixed manufacturing cost is expensed as the cost of maintaining the capacity to produce. As a result, management is better able to make short-term decisions relating to profitability and the product mix.

explanations.A: Which results in higher operating income during a given period depends on whether production exceeds sales or sales exceeds production during that period. When production is greater than sales, operating income under absorption costing will be higher than operating income under variable costing. When production is less than sales, operating income under variable costing will be higher than operating income under absorption costing. Nevertheless, no accounting decision should be made to achieve a specific reporting objective such as higher operating income. The only justifiable reason for any accounting decision such as use of variable costing for internal financial reporting should be for the purpose of improving the financial reporting and making it more useful.
explanations.B: Variable costing is not acceptable for income tax reporting purposes. Absorption costing is required on the company's income tax return.
explanations.C: It is true that all costs are variable in the long term. However, this has nothing to do with a reason for using variable costing.

studyUnit: Study Unit 11: D.3. Variable and Absorption Costing

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Xylon Company uses direct (variable) costing for internal reporting and absorption costing for the external financial statements. A review of the firm’s internal and external disclosures will likely find

options.A: a higher inventoriable unit cost reported to management than to the shareholders.
options.B: a difference in the treatment of fixed selling and administrative costs.
options.C: a contribution margin rather than gross margin in the reports released to shareholders.
options.D: internal income figures that vary closely with sales and external income figures that are influenced by both units sold and productive output.

correctExplanation: Internal income statements using variable costing -- at least the contribution margin -- would vary closely with sales, because only variable costs are considered product costs when variable costing is used. Fixed factory overhead is expensed as it is incurred. External income figures using absorption costing would vary with the relationship between units produced and units sold. When production is greater than sales, net income under absorption costing is higher than it is under variable costing because the fixed factory overheads are inventoried under this method. Fixed factory overhead attached to units produced but not sold remains in inventory and thus the fixed costs attached to those units is not expensed until the units are sold. When sales are greater than production, net income under variable costing is higher than it is under absorption costing. Under absorption costing, the fixed factory overhead attached to the units sold is expensed (along with other product costs) as cost of goods sold. Because beginning inventory is sold when sales are greater than production, fixed factory overhead costs from the previous year are expensed in the current year under absorption costing whereas under variable costing, they would have been expensed during the previous year when they were incurred. As a result, net income will be higher under variable costing.

explanations.A: A higher inventoriable unit cost would be reported to shareholders than to management, because fixed manufacturing costs are inventoriable costs under absorption costing but are period costs under variable costing.
explanations.B: Fixed selling and administrative costs are treated the same way under variable and absorption costing: as period costs.
explanations.C: The contribution margin would be in the reports released to management. The reports released to shareholders would show a gross profit margin instead of a contribution margin.

studyUnit: Study Unit 11: D.3. Variable and Absorption Costing

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: When a firm prepares financial reports using absorption costing:

options.A: Profits may decrease with increased sales even if there is no change in selling prices and costs.
options.B: Profits will always increase with increases in sales.
options.C: Profits will always decrease with decreases in sales.
options.D: Decreased output and constant sales result in increased profits.

correctExplanation: When absorption costing is being used and sales are greater than production, operating income will be lower than it would be under variable costing, because some of the fixed costs incurred in a previous period and capitalized in inventory at that time will be expensed in cost of goods sold along with the current period’s fixed costs. Under variable costing, only the current period’s fixed costs would have been expensed.

explanations.B: This will not always be the case when using absorption costing.
explanations.C: This will not always be the case when using absorption costing.
explanations.D: This will not always be the case when using absorption costing.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: When comparing absorption costing with variable costing, the difference in operating income can be explained by the difference between the

options.A: ending inventory in units and the beginning inventory in units, multiplied by the budgeted fixed manufacturing cost per unit.
options.B: units sold and the units produced, multiplied by the budgeted variable manufacturing cost per unit.
options.C: ending inventory in units and the beginning inventory in units, multiplied by the unit sales price.
options.D: units sold and the units produced, multiplied by the unit sales price.

correctExplanation: This is an example of a question where the answer that would be exactly correct is not given. However, the best answer from among the answer choices given is "ending inventory in units and the beginning inventory in units, multiplied by the budgeted fixed manufacturing cost per unit." That is the best answer because it is the only answer choice that references fixed manufacturing cost. The difference between absorption costing and variable costing is in the treatment of fixed manufacturing costs. This answer is not exactly correct because it does not take into consideration the accounting treatment of the variances between the actual fixed overhead cost and the budgeted fixed overhead cost in absorption costing. Nor does it take into consideration the fact that the company might be using the FIFO inventory cost flow assumption. If it is using FIFO, the fixed cost in the beginning inventory that is sold first is the cost of the previous year when the beginning inventory was manufactured, which is probably a different cost from the current year’s cost.

explanations.B: The difference in operating income between variable costing and absorption costing is in the treatment of fixed manufacturing costs.
explanations.C: The difference in operating income between variable costing and absorption costing is in the treatment of fixed manufacturing costs.
explanations.D: The difference in operating income between variable costing and absorption costing is in the treatment of fixed manufacturing costs.

studyUnit: Study Unit 11: D.3. Variable and Absorption Costing

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Huntington Corporation pays bonuses to its managers based on operating income, as calculated under variable costing. It is now two months before year-end, and earnings have been depressed for some time. Which one of the following actions should Wanda Richards, production manager, implement if she desires to maximize her bonus for this year?

options.A: Postpone $1.8 million of discretionary equipment maintenance until next year.
options.B: Implement, with the aid of the controller, an activity-based costing system.
options.C: Step up production so that more manufacturing costs are deferred into inventory.
options.D: Eliminate $2.3 million of advertising and marketing costs.

correctExplanation: All of the listed actions are targeted to increase operating income; however, cutting $2.3 million of advertising and marketing costs is beyond the control of the production manager. In addition, stepping up production to defer manufacturing costs into inventory would work only under absorption costing. Finally, ABC and ABM systems implementation is beneficial in the long-run, but would have little effect in the current short-term period. Thus, postponing equipment maintenance until the next reporting period is the only action that would affect operating income and the production managers’ year-end bonus.

explanations.B: ABC systems implementation is beneficial in the long-run, but would have little effect in the current short-term period.
explanations.C: Stepping up production to defer manufacturing costs into inventory would work only under absorption costing.
explanations.D: Cutting $2.3 million of advertising and marketing costs is beyond the control of the production manager.

studyUnit: Study Unit 11: D.3. Variable and Absorption Costing

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing - Theory Questions
question: Dawn Company has significant fixed overhead costs in the manufacturing of its sole product, auto mufflers. For internal reporting purposes, in which one of the following situations would the value of ending finished goods inventory be higher under direct (variable) costing rather than under absorption costing?

options.A: In all cases when ending finished goods inventory exists.
options.B: If more units were sold than were produced during a given year.
options.C: If more units were produced than were sold during a given year.
options.D: None of these situations.

correctExplanation: In all cases, the value of ending finished goods inventory will be higher under absorption costing, not variable costing. An allocation of fixed manufacturing cost is included in inventoried goods under absorption costing whereas under variable costing it is not because the fixed manufacturing cost is expensed as incurred under variable costing. Therefore, there is no situation in which the value of ending finished goods inventory would be higher under variable costing than under absorption costing.

explanations.A: In all cases when ending finished goods inventory exists, the value of ending finished goods inventory will be higher under absorption costing, not variable costing.
explanations.B: This would not cause the value of ending finished goods inventory to be higher under direct (variable) costing than under absorption costing. If more units were sold than were produced during a given year, that would cause operating income to be higher under variable costing, but it would not cause the value of ending finished goods inventory to be higher under variable costing.
explanations.C: This would not cause the value of ending finished goods inventory to be higher under direct (variable) costing than under absorption costing. If more units were produced than were sold during a given year, that would cause operating income to be higher under absorption costing, but it would not cause the value of ending finished goods inventory to be higher under variable costing. topic: Variable and Absorption Costing – Calculation Questions
question: An exercise equipment manufacturer uses the variable costing method and has determined that the total manufacturing cost of its single 30-pound barbell is $27 per unit. The direct material cost per unit is $16. The allocated administration expenses are $6 per unit. The allocated fixed rental costs are $3 per unit. If no other costs are incurred, the direct labor cost per unit is
correctExplanation: Under variable costing, only variable costs are allocated to production. Fixed factory overheads are reported as period costs and are expensed in the period in which they are incurred, so the allocated fixed rental costs are not allocated to units produced. Administration expenses are always expensed as incurred regardless of what method of costing is being used. Therefore, the direct labor cost allocated to each unit under variable costing is the difference between the total manufacturing cost of $27 and the direct material cost of $16 allocated per unit, which is $11.

explanations.A: This cost for direct labor is incorrect. This is the total manufacturing cost of $27 minus the direct material cost of $16 allocated per unit and minus the allocated fixed rental cost of $3 per unit and minus the allocated administration expenses of $6 per unit. Under variable costing, only variable manufacturing costs are allocated to production. Fixed factory overheads are not allocated to units produced. Administration expenses are always expensed as incurred regardless of what method of costing is being used. So the allocated fixed rental expense and the allocated administration expenses should not be deducted from the total manufacturing cost to calculate the direct labor cost. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: This cost for direct labor is incorrect. This is the total manufacturing cost of $27 minus the direct material cost of $16 allocated per unit and minus the allocated administration expenses of $6 per unit. Administration expenses are always period costs that are expensed as incurred, so the administration expenses should not be deducted from the total manufacturing cost to calculate direct labor cost. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: This cost for direct labor is incorrect. This is the total manufacturing cost of $27 minus the direct material cost of $16 allocated per unit and minus the allocated fixed rental cost of $3 per unit. Under variable costing, only variable manufacturing costs are allocated to production. Fixed factory overheads are not allocated to units produced under variable costing, so the allocated fixed rental cost should not be deducted from total manufacturing costs to calculate direct labor cost. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing – Calculation Questions
question: Almax Corporation produces and sells smart phones. The following information relates to Almax’s operations for the last year. Variable cost per unit $5.20 Total fixed manufacturing overhead cost $260,000 Total fixed selling and administrative cost $180,000 Units produced and sold 400,000 Using absorption costing, what was Almax's cost per unit last year?
intro: Almax Corporation produces and sells smart phones. The following information relates to Almax’s operations for the last year.
table: Total fixed selling and administrative cost
tail: Using absorption costing, what was Almax's cost per unit last year?
correctExplanation: The cost per unit using absorption costing is the total product costs, which include the variable cost per unit and the fixed manufacturing overhead applied to each unit. The variable cost per unit is given as $5.20. The fixed manufacturing overhead applied per unit is the total fixed manufacturing overhead of $260,000 divided by the number of units produced, which is 400,000, so the fixed overhead applied per unit is $0.65. The total cost per unit using absorption costing is $5.20 + $0.65 = $5.85.

explanations.B: This is the variable cost per unit of $5.20 minus the fixed manufacturing overhead cost per unit of $0.65 ($260,000 ÷ 400,000) plus the fixed selling and administrative cost per unit of $0.45 ($180,000 ÷ 400,000). The cost per unit using absorption costing is the total product costs, which include the variable cost per unit and the fixed manufacturing overhead applied to each unit. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: This is the variable cost per unit of $5.20 plus fixed manufacturing overhead applied of $0.65 per unit ($260,000 ÷ 400,000), plus fixed selling and administrative cost per unit of $0.45 ($180,000 ÷ 400,000). The cost per unit using absorption costing is the total product costs, and selling and administrative costs are not product costs. Selling and administrative costs are period costs that are expensed as they are incurred. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: This is the variable cost per unit of $5.20 minus the fixed manufacturing overhead applied per unit of $0.65 ($260,000 ÷ 400,000). The applied fixed overhead should be added to the variable cost, not subtracted from it. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing – Calculation Questions
question: During the month of May, Robinson Corporation sold 1,000 units. The cost per unit for May was as follows. Cost Per Unit Direct materials $5.50 Direct labor 3.00 Variable manufacturing overhead 1.00 Fixed manufacturing overhead 1.50 Fixed administrative costs 3.50 Total $15.00 May's income using absorption costing was $9,500. The income for May if variable costing had been used would have been $9,125. The number of units Robinson produced during May was
intro: During the month of May, Robinson Corporation sold 1,000 units. The cost per unit for May was as follows. Cost Per Unit
tail: May's income using absorption costing was $9,500. The income for May if variable costing had been used would have been $9,125. The number of units Robinson produced during May was

options.A: 1,075 units.
options.B: 750 units.
options.C: 1,250 units.
options.D: 925 units.

correctExplanation: The difference between net income under absorption costing and net income under variable costing is fixed manufacturing overhead. Under variable costing, all of the fixed manufacturing overhead will be expensed. Under absorption costing, fixed manufacturing overhead for the units that were sold will be expensed, but fixed manufacturing overhead for units manufactured but not sold will be in inventory. According to the information given in the problem, the difference between Robinson's net income under absorption costing and its net income under variable costing is $9,500 − $9,125, which is $375. Fixed manufacturing overhead cost was $1.50 per unit. Dividing $375 by $1.50 per unit gives us the number of units that were not expensed under absorption costing, which is 250. The fixed manufacturing cost for those 250 units ($375) remained in inventory because those 250 units were not sold. The company sold 1,000 units. If 1,000 units were sold and 250 units were not sold but remained in inventory, the total produced was 1,000 + 250, or 1,250.

explanations.A: This answer results from dividing the difference between net income using absorption costing and net income using variable costing ($375) by total fixed costs of $5.00 per unit to calculate the number of units that were unsold. The result, 75 units, was then added to the 1,000 units that were sold to calculate the number of units produced. The process was correct, but only fixed manufacturing overhead of $1.50 per unit should have been used to calculate the number of unsold units. Fixed administrative costs are period costs and are expensed as incurred.
explanations.B: This answer results from subtracting the number of unsold units from the sold units (1,000 − 250 = 750) instead of adding the unsold units to the sold units to calculate the number of units produced.
explanations.D: This answer results from dividing the difference between net income using absorption costing and net income using variable costing ($375) by total fixed costs of $5.00 per unit to calculate the number of units that were unsold. The result, 75 units, was then subtracted from the 1,000 units that were sold to calculate the number of units produced. This is incorrect for two reasons: (1) Only fixed manufacturing overhead of $1.50 per unit should have been used to calculate the number of unsold units. Fixed administrative costs are period costs and are expensed as incurred. And (2) the number of unsold units should be added to, not subtracted from, the number of units sold to calculate the number of units produced.

topic: Variable and Absorption Costing – Calculation Questions
question: During the first month of its operations, a company manufactured a product with variable production costs of $50 per unit. Fixed manufacturing overhead totaled $1,800,000 and is allocated based upon units produced. During the month, the company completed 15,000 units, sold 12,000 units, and incurred no variances. If the company’s operating income under absorption costing was $400,000, its operating income (loss) under variable costing was
correctExplanation: Under variable costing, the fixed manufacturing costs are fully expensed during the period. Under absorption costing, the fixed manufacturing costs are allocated to the units that are produced. The difference in operating income between the two methods can be calculated by multiplying the amount of fixed overhead per unit by the amount of the change in inventory during the period. During the period, inventory increased. This means that under absorption costing some of the fixed manufacturing costs are included in inventory at the end of the period and have not been expensed. So, we know that because inventory increased during the period the variable method will give a lower operating income. The fixed overhead per unit for the period is $120. This is calculated as the fixed manufacturing amount of $1,800,000 divided by the number of units produced, 15,000. Multiplying the amount of fixed overhead allocated to each unit by the number of units by which inventory increased, we calculate that there is $360,000 of fixed manufacturing costs on the balance sheet under absorption costing. This means that operating income under variable costing would be $360,000 less than the $400,000 operating income under variable costing, or $40,000.

explanations.B: This answer results from assuming that variable manufacturing costs are treated the same way as fixed manufacturing costs under both variable costing and absorption costing. Since the fixed manufacturing costs for the unsold units would be in ending inventory under absorption costing but expensed under variable costing, this answer assumes the variable manufacturing costs for the unsold units are also in inventory at the end of the period under absorption costing but expensed as incurred under variable costing. However, the variable manufacturing costs for the unsold units are in inventory at the end of the period under both absorption costing and variable costing. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: This answer incorrectly allocates the fixed manufacturing costs to the number of units sold instead of the number of units produced. See the correct answer for a full explanation of the calculation of operating income under the variable costing method.
explanations.D: This answer adds the difference between the two methods instead of subtracting it. See the correct answer for a full explanation of the calculation of operating income under the variable costing method.

question: Product sales: 1,000 units at $10 each Variable manufacturing costs: $5.50 per unit Fixed manufacturing overhead (planned and actual): $1,200 Fixed selling and administrative costs: $1,000 Units produced (planned and actual): 1,200 Operating income under variable (direct) costing is
intro: Product sales: 1,000 units at $10 each Variable manufacturing costs: $5.50 per unit
tail: Operating income under variable (direct) costing is
correctExplanation: Under variable costing, all of the fixed factory overheads will be expensed during the period. The manufacturing contribution per unit is calculated as the sales price ($10) minus the variable costs of production ($5.50) and is $4.50. Since they sold 1,000 units, this gave them $4,500 of manufacturing contribution margin. Variable selling and administrative costs are $0.50 per unit sold. Therefore, the contribution margin (sales revenue minus all variable costs, including both manufacturing and non-manufacturing) is thus $4.50 per unit minus $0.50 per unit, or $4.00 per unit, which equals $4,000 in total. Fixed manufacturing ($1,200) and fixed selling ($1,000) costs are subtracted from the contribution margin, giving us a net operating income of $1,800 ($4,000 − $1,200 − $1,000).

explanations.B: This answer results from multiplying the variable manufacturing cost per unit by the number of units produced instead of by the number of units sold.
explanations.C: This answer results from multiplying the variable manufacturing cost per unit and the variable selling and administrative cost per unit by the number of units produced instead of by the number of units sold.
explanations.D: This answer results from not deducting the variable selling and administrative costs.

question: Product sales: 1,000 units at $10 each Variable manufacturing costs: $5.50 per unit Fixed manufacturing overhead (planned and actual): $1,200 Fixed selling and administrative costs: $1,000 Units produced (planned and actual): 1,200 Assuming operating income under variable costing is $1,800, operating income under absorption costing is
intro: Product sales: 1,000 units at $10 each Variable manufacturing costs: $5.50 per unit
tail: Assuming operating income under variable costing is $1,800, operating income under absorption costing is
correctExplanation: There are two ways that we can solve this problem. The first is to calculate a full absorption costing income statement, as follows: Per Unit × Units Sold Total Sales revenue $10.00 1,000 $10,000 Cost of goods sold: Variable COGS 5.50 1,000 5,500 Fixed COGS 1.001 1,000 Gross profit $3.50 1,000 $3,500 Variable S & A expense .50 1,000 500 Fixed S & A expense 1,000 Net operating income $2,000 1$1,200 fixed cost ÷ 1,200 units produced. The second way is to use the differences between variable and absorption costing to calculate the difference between the two methods. Since we are given the variable costing income, we can then back into the absorption costing income. The difference between variable and absorption costing is the treatment of fixed manufacturing overhead. Under variable costing it is expensed, but under absorption costing it is treated as a product cost. Since the fixed factory overheads were $1,200 and they produced 1,200 units, the fixed factory overhead per unit was $1. Since production was 1,200 units and sales were only 1,000 units, inventory increased by 200 units. This means that the fixed factory overhead related to those 200 units is not on the income statement, but on the balance sheet. Since beginning inventory was zero, we know that operating income under the absorption costing method will be $200 higher than the variable method income, or $2,000. (Note: this was possible because beginning inventory was zero. If beginning inventory were not zero, we might not be able to find the answer this way.)

explanations.B: This answer results from treating the fixed selling and administrative costs as product costs. Fixed selling and administrative costs are period costs and are expensed as incurred.
explanations.C: This is the operating income under variable costing.
explanations.D: This answer results from two errors: (1) Treating the fixed selling and administrative costs as product costs. Fixed selling and administrative costs are period costs and are expensed as incurred. And (2) treating the fixed manufacturing cost as a period cost. Under absorption costing, fixed manufacturing overhead is applied to units of production, and the cost for unsold units remains in inventory and is not expensed.

question: Mill Corporation had the following unit costs for the recently concluded calendar year, which are the same as its unit costs for the year previous to the recently concluded year. Variable Fixed Manufacturing $8.00 $3.00 Nonmanufacturing $2.00 $5.50 Inventory for Mill's sole product totaled 6,000 units on January 1 and 5,200 units on December 31. Mill Corporation uses the first in-first out cost flow assumption. When compared to variable costing income, Mill's absorption costing income is
intro: Mill Corporation had the following unit costs for the recently concluded calendar year, which are the same as its unit costs for the year previous to the recently concluded year. Variable Fixed
tail: Inventory for Mill's sole product totaled 6,000 units on January 1 and 5,200 units on December 31. Mill Corporation uses the first in-first out cost flow assumption. When compared to variable costing income, Mill's absorption costing income is

options.A: $6,800 lower.
options.B: $2,400 higher.
options.C: $6,800 higher.
options.D: $2,400 lower.

correctExplanation: Mill’s inventory decreased during the year from 6,000 units on Jan. 1 to 5,200 units on December 31. Therefore, we know that Mill sold 800 more units than it manufactured during the recently concluded calendar year. Total fixed manufacturing cost in inventory on Jan. 1 was 6,000 × $3 = $18,000. Total fixed manufacturing cost in inventory on Dec. 31 was 5,200 × $3, or $15,600. The difference between $18,000 and $15,600, which is $2,400, was transferred to cost of goods sold as an expense under absorption costing. Under variable costing, though, that $2,400 would have been expensed during the previous year as fixed costs for that year, and thus it would not have been on the recently concluded year’s income statement, so net income under variable costing would have been $2,400 higher than under absorption costing. Therefore, net income under absorption costing would be $2,400 lower than it would be under variable costing.

explanations.A: This is the total fixed costs, both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing, multiplied by the amount of decrease in inventory. Nonmanufacturing fixed costs are expensed as they are incurred under both variable and absorption costing, so they could not have accounted for any part of the difference in net income.
explanations.B: This is the fixed manufacturing cost per unit multiplied by the number of units by which inventory decreased during the year. However, the effect of the inventory decrease on net income under absorption costing is to decrease net income, not increase it, as compared with variable costing. See the correct answer for a full explanation.
explanations.C: This is the total fixed costs, both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing, multiplied by the amount of decrease in inventory. Nonmanufacturing fixed costs are expensed as they are incurred under both variable and absorption costing, so they could not have accounted for any part of the difference in net income.

question: During its first year of operations, a company produced 275,000 units and sold 250,000 units. The following costs were incurred during the year: Variable costs per unit Direct materials $15.00 Direct labor 10.00 Manufacturing overhead 12.50 Selling and administrative 2.50 Manufacturing overhead $2,200,000 Selling and administrative 1,375,000 What is the difference between operating income calculated on the absorption costing basis and on the variable costing basis?
intro: During its first year of operations, a company produced 275,000 units and sold 250,000 units. The following costs were incurred during the year: Variable costs per unit
tail: What is the difference between operating income calculated on the absorption costing basis and on the variable costing basis?

options.A: Variable costing operating income is greater than absorption costing operating income by $62,500.
options.B: Absorption costing operating income is greater than variable costing operating income by $220,000.
options.C: Absorption costing operating income is greater than variable costing operating income by $325,000.
options.D: Absorption costing operating income is greater than variable costing operating income by $200,000.

correctExplanation: We know that the number of units in inventory increased during the period, so we know that absorption costing income will be greater than variable costing income. The question we have left is by how much. The only difference between the two methods is in the treatment of fixed factory overheads. Under absorption costing the fixed factory overheads are allocated to the units produced and under variable costing they are expensed. Because this is the first year of operations we can simply multiply the fixed factory overhead per unit by the increase in inventory to determine the difference between the two methods. There was $2,200,000 of fixed factory overhead that was applied to the 275,000 units produced. This is $8 per unit. Inventory increased by 25,000 units, so the difference between the two methods would be $200,000 (25,000 units × $8 per unit). Because these $200,000 in fixed costs are on the balance sheet under absorption costing but expensed under variable costing, operating income will be higher under absorption costing.

explanations.A: Absorption costing will give a higher income and the difference will be a different amount from this answer.
explanations.B: Though the absorption costing income will be higher, it is not higher by this amount. This answer allocates the fixed costs based on the number of units sold.
explanations.C: Though the absorption costing income will be higher, it is not higher by this amount. This answer includes the fixed selling and administrative costs as a product cost.
