topic: Variable and Absorption Costing – Calculation Questions
question: Merlene Company uses a standard cost accounting system. Data for the last fiscal year are as follows. Units Beginning inventory of finished goods 100 Production during the year 700 Sales 750 Ending inventory of finished goods 50 Product selling price $200 Standard variable manufacturing cost 90 Budgeted selling and administrative costs (all fixed) $45,000 *Denominator level of activity is 750 units for the year. There were no price, efficiency, or spending variances for the year, and actual selling and administrative expenses equaled the budget amounts. The previous year's variable manufacturing costs per unit were the same as the current year's budgeted and actual variable manufacturing costs per unit. Any volume variance is written off to cost of goods sold in the year incurred. There are no work-in-process inventories. The amount of operating income earned by Merlene for the last fiscal year using variable costing was
intro: Merlene Company uses a standard cost accounting system. Data for the last fiscal year are as follows. Units
table: Budgeted selling and administrative costs (all fixed)
tail: *Denominator level of activity is 750 units for the year. There were no price, efficiency, or spending variances for the year, and actual selling and administrative expenses equaled the budget amounts. The previous year's variable manufacturing costs per unit were the same as the current year's budgeted and actual variable manufacturing costs per unit. Any volume variance is written off to cost of goods sold in the year incurred. There are no work-in-process inventories. The amount of operating income earned by Merlene for the last fiscal year using variable costing was
correctExplanation: Since there were no price, efficiency or spending variances, that means actual costs per unit were the same as the standard costs per unit for the year. Thus, we can use the standard costs per unit given as actual amounts for purposes of calculating operating income under variable costing. Income statements are based on the number of units sold, not on the number of units produced. The company produced 700 units and sold 750 units, so they sold 50 units from their beginning inventory, and the cost of those units needs to be included in the cost of goods sold. Beginning inventory is costed at the previous year's costs; and since the previous year's variable costs per unit were the same as the current year's budgeted and actual costs, we can use the current year's variable manufacturing costs for all 750 units sold. Under variable costing, only variable manufacturing costs are inventoried, while fixed manufacturing costs are expensed as incurred. The problem says there were no spending variances, and therefore we know that the fixed manufacturing cost incurred was the same as the fixed manufacturing cost budgeted. Therefore, we can use the standard fixed manufacturing cost per unit and the denominator level of activity to calculate the total fixed manufacturing overhead that was budgeted, and we will also have the actual fixed manufacturing overhead that was incurred. We know that the standard fixed manufacturing cost per unit ($20) was calculated by dividing the total budgeted fixed manufacturing cost by the anticipated production of 750 units. Therefore, we can multiply the $20 per unit standard cost by the anticipated production of 750 units, and we will have the budgeted total fixed manufacturing cost. As we said, since there were no spending variances for the year, the actual fixed manufacturing cost is the same as the budgeted fixed manufacturing cost, and the full amount of the actual fixed manufacturing cost, or $15,000, is expensed. Actual selling and administrative cost is the same as the budgeted selling and administrative cost, so that is used as given. And since there were no production variances, no variances needed to be written off to cost of goods sold, so that is an adjustment that does not need to be made. The income statement using variable costing was Sales revenue: 750 units @ $200 $150,000 Variable cost: 750 units @ $90 67,500 Contribution margin $ 82,500 Fixed mfg. cost: $20 standard cost × 750 (denomin. level of activity) $ 15,000 Selling and administrative cost 45,000 Net operating income $ 22,500

explanations.B: This is an attempt to calculate operating income under the absorption costing method by calculating operating income under the variable costing method and then adjusting it by fixed manufacturing costs using the shortcut method of multiplying the fixed overhead cost per unit by the number of units of change in inventory. There are several problems with this approach. 1) The question does not ask for operating income under the absorption costing method. The question asks for operating income under variable costing. 2) Even if absorption costing operating income was desired, the shortcut method cannot be used to calculate operating income under the absorption costing method because that method can be used only if (a) beginning inventory is zero (it is not); (b) the LIFO inventory cost flow assumption is being used and ending inventory is higher than beginning inventory (neither of those are true in this situation); or (c) beginning inventories are valued at the same per-unit fixed manufacturing cost as the current year's planned per-unit fixed manufacturing cost (the question does not state what the fixed manufacturing cost was in the former year, so the fixed manufacturing cost in beginning inventory is unknown). 3) In fact, operating income under the absorption costing method cannot be calculated based on the facts given. Fifty units were sold from beginning inventory, but the question does not give the fixed cost per unit that was applied during the previous year. topic: Variable and Absorption Costing – Calculation Questions
question: Using absorption costing, Langdon Company's income for October was $250,000. Langdon began the month with 10,000 units in finished goods inventory that contained $30,000 of fixed manufacturing overhead costs. During October, the company produced 330,000 units and sold 325,000 units. The fixed manufacturing overhead for October totaled $990,000. If Langdon Company had used variable costing, its income for October would be
correctExplanation: Inventory increased by 5,000 units during October, from 10,000 units to 15,000, calculated as follows: Beginning inventory 10,000 Plus units manufactured 330,000 Less units sold 325,000 Ending inventory 15,000 If variable costing had been used, the fixed manufacturing overhead that was incurred and applied to those 5,000 additional units in ending inventory would have been expensed instead. Fixed manufacturing overhead was $3 per unit for the units in beginning inventory and for the units produced during October, as follows: Fixed manufacturing overhead in beginning inventory: $30,000 ÷ 10,000 units = $3 per unit. Fixed manufacturing overhead in October production: $990,000 ÷ 330,000 units = $3 per unit. Since the amount of fixed manufacturing overhead was the same for the units in beginning inventory as for the units produced during the period ($3 per unit), operating income for October under variable costing can be calculated by reducing operating income under absorption costing by $3 per unit multiplied by the number of units by which inventory increased during the period. Therefore, if variable costing had been used, October expenses would have been $15,000 higher (5,000 × $3) and operating income for October would have been $15,000 lower than under absorption costing. Operating income would have been $250,000 − $15,000 = $235,000.

explanations.A: This is the operating income under absorption costing that is given in the question. Operating income under variable costing is different because the fixed manufacturing costs that were applied to the unsold units manufactured during the period that remained in ending inventory is expensed as a period cost under variable costing. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: This is the October operating income under absorption costing adjusted by the $3 per unit of fixed manufacturing costs per unit multiplied by the 15,000 units in ending inventory. Since the amount of fixed manufacturing overhead was the same for the units in beginning inventory as for the units produced during the period ($3 per unit), operating income for October under variable costing can be calculated by reducing operating income under absorption costing by $3 per unit multiplied by the number of units by which inventory increased during the period, but not by all the units in ending inventory.
explanations.C: This answer results from adding to the operating income under absorption costing the fixed manufacturing overhead that was incurred and applied to the increased number of units in ending inventory instead of deducting it from the operating income under absorption costing. When variable costing is used, all fixed manufacturing overhead cost incurred during the period, including that applied to units manufactured during the period but unsold, is expensed as period costs. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: Nance Corp began operations in January. The company produced 50,000 units and sold 45,000 units in its first year of operations. intro: Nance Corp began operations in January. The company produced 50,000 units and sold 45,000 units in its first year of operations. Costs for the year were as follows:
tail: How would the operating income of Nance compare between the variable method and full absorption costing methods?

options.A: Absorption would be $25,000 higher.
options.B: Absorption would be $32,500 higher.

options.D: Variable would be $25,000 higher.

correctExplanation: The difference between the two methods relates only to the fixed manufacturing overhead costs. Because this was the company’s first year of operations and thus beginning inventory was zero, the amount of the difference can be calculated as follows: Fixed manufacturing costs per unit × Change in the level of inventory Fixed manufacturing costs divided by 50,000 units produced equals fixed manufacturing cost per unit of $5. options.A: Equal to Year 2.
options.B: Equal to Year 1.
options.C: Greater than Year 2.

correctExplanation: Gross profit is calculated as net sales revenue minus cost of goods sold. Since all of the costs have remained the same over the period and there has been no change in inventory for any period (since sales have been equal to production each year), the gross profit for Year 3 will be equal to the gross profit from the year in which sales were the same level, and this is Year 1. Because this is a new company and for every year since its beginning, sales have been equal to production, inventory at year end for each year has been zero. Because of this, we do not need to know whether the company closes out under- and over-applied overhead to cost of goods sold only, or whether the company prorates it between cost of goods sold and inventory. Since inventory is zero, all under- or over-applied overhead will have been closed to cost of goods sold only. And for each year since its beginning, the company has had under-applied fixed overhead, because actual production has been lower than planned production. Unless fixed overhead has been very different in Year 3 than it was in Year 1, the gross profit for the two years should be substantially the same.

Sales in Year 3 are lower than in Year 2. Since prices and costs have remained the same and sales have equaled production each year, the gross profit for Year 3, a year in which sales decreased from the previous year, cannot be equal to the gross profit for Year 2.

Since prices and costs have remained the same and sales have equaled production each year, gross profit for Year 3 cannot be greater than the gross profit for Year 1.

correctExplanation: This problem does not specify whether Valyn is using a standard cost system (in which standard, or planned, costs are used to account for production) or an actual cost system (in which actual costs are used). However, it does say that Valyn uses a predetermined manufacturing overhead rate for applying manufacturing overhead to its product. Under the absorption method fixed manufacturing overheads are applied to the units produced at the predetermined rate, whereas under the variable method, they are expensed. The fixed factory overhead cost applied per unit is $5 and we can determine the difference between these two methods by multiplying this $5 per unit difference by the number of units that were added to inventory during the period. Inventory increased by 5,000 units, calculated as follows: Beginning Inventory 35,000 Units + 130,000 Units Produced − 125,000 Units Sold = Ending Inventory 40,000 Units. Thus, the predetermined fixed overhead rate of $5 per unit that was applied to each unit as it was manufactured is attached to the 5,000 units that were added to inventory and was not expensed under absorption costing. 5,000 × $5 gives us a $25,000 difference in income between the two methods. Note that the difference in operating income can be calculated in this way only because The beginning finished goods inventory is valued at the same per unit manufacturing cost as the current year's planned per unit manufacturing cost (which implies that the fixed manufacturing cost in beginning inventory was the same as the current year's predetermined application rate per unit for fixed manufacturing overhead); Over- or under-applied manufacturing overhead is closed to the cost of goods sold account at the end of the period; and There is no beginning work-in-process inventory. If any one of those factors had not been present, we would not have been able to calculate the difference between the two methods in this way.

The underapplied fixed manufacturing overhead is not relevant to the calculation of the difference in operating income between absorption costing and variable costing, because it is handled the same way under both methods. The $65,000 underapplied fixed manufacturing cost is charged to expense under absorption costing because the problem says that underapplied or overapplied manufacturing overhead is closed out to cost of goods sold. It is also charged to expense under variable costing, because under variable costing, all fixed costs incurred are expensed as period costs as incurred. Since the amount of underapplied fixed manufacturing overhead under absorption costing is handled the same way under both methods, it is not relevant to a calculation of the difference in operating income between them.
explanations.B: This answer results from including fixed administrative expenses along with fixed manufacturing overhead in calculating the fixed cost that would be included in ending inventory under absorption costing but not included under variable costing. Fixed administrative costs (along with fixed selling costs) are expensed in both methods, so the fixed administrative costs do not contribute to the difference between operating income under absorption costing and under variable costing.
explanations.C: This is the amount of underapplied fixed manufacturing overhead. It is not the difference in operating income between the absorption costing and the variable costing methods.

However, it does say that Valyn uses a predetermined manufacturing overhead rate for applying manufacturing overhead to its product. And since the actual, incurred per unit costs for direct materials, direct labor and variable manufacturing overhead are exactly the same as the planned per unit costs for those items, we do not need to know whether standard costing or actual costing is being used in order to answer this question. (To verify that the actual variable costs per unit are exactly the same as the planned per unit costs, multiply the planned per unit cost for each of those items by the actual production of 130,000 units. Under absorption costing, the per unit cost of inventory includes all production costs, both fixed and variable. These costs are applied to each unit as it is produced, and the costs go into inventory until the units the costs are attached to are sold. When the units are sold, the costs attached to each sold unit are expensed. The difference between the actual incurred costs and the applied costs for fixed manufacturing overhead is a variance, also called under-applied or over-applied costs. The problem says that this variance is closed out at the end of the period by debiting or crediting the whole amount to cost of goods sold. Thus, for each unit that is sold, $5 of fixed manufacturing overhead is expensed as cost of goods sold. 125,000 units were sold, so this is $625,000 fixed manufacturing costs in cost of goods sold related to the units sold. Since under- or over-applied overhead is allocated to cost of goods sold, we need to calculate the amount of the under- or over-applied overhead. A total of $650,000 of fixed overhead was applied during the period (130,000 units produced at $5 fixed manufacturing cost applied per unit). The actual fixed overhead was $715,000, so fixed overhead was under-applied by $65,000. This $65,000 of under-applied overhead will be added to cost of goods sold expense. Also, all of the fixed selling and fixed administrative costs were expensed during the period because these are period costs. These costs total $1,405,000. Under absorption costing, the total fixed costs expensed therefore equals $625,000 + $65,000 + $1,405,000, or $2,095,000.

explanations.A: This answer assumes that the fixed overhead applied was applied only to the units that were sold, and not to the number of units that were produced.
explanations.C: The problem says that any over- or under-applied manufacturing overhead is closed to the Cost of Goods Sold account at the end of the reporting year. This answer omits that adjustment.

This is incorrect for two reasons: (1) The problem says that any over- or under-applied manufacturing overhead is closed to the Cost of Goods Sold account at the end of the reporting year. This answer omits that adjustment. (2) The fixed manufacturing cost expensed should be the $5 per unit fixed manufacturing cost multiplied by the number of units sold, not the number of units produced.

question: A company is setting up a new division to sell its products in Africa. An accountant has determined that the new African division will have to sell 250,000 units in order to cover the division’s fixed costs of $365,000. The company is estimating total sales of $475,000 for the new African division. What is the contribution margin per unit for the new African division?
correctExplanation: In a variable income statement, the contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs. Contribution margin minus fixed costs equals operating income. To cover its fixed costs, the African division's contribution margin must be equal to its fixed costs, which are planned at $365,000. Since the new African division will need to sell 250,000 units in order to cover the division’s fixed costs, the contribution margin per unit sold must be $365,000 ÷ 250,000, or $1.46.

explanations.B: This is the variable cost per unit. It is calculated as the total revenue of $475,000 minus the contribution margin required to cover the fixed costs of $365,000, the difference of $110,000 divided by the 250,000 units that will need to be sold to cover the fixed cost. Contribution margin per unit is the sales revenue per unit minus the variable costs per unit.
explanations.C: This is total sales of $475,000 divided by the 250,000 sales required to cover the division's fixed costs. This is the sales revenue per unit, or the sales price per unit that will need to be charged. Contribution margin per unit is the sales revenue per unit minus the variable costs per unit.
explanations.D: This is the 250,000 units sold divided by $365,000, the African division's contribution margin required to cover its fixed costs of $365,000. question: In allocating factory service department costs to producing departments, which one of the following items would most likely be used as an activity base?

options.A: Salary of service department employees.
options.B: Units of product sold.
options.C: Units of electric power consumed.
options.D: Direct materials usage.

correctExplanation: The activity base used for the allocation of service department costs should represent the usage of the service department services by the user departments. The amount of power consumed is the best of the choices given for allocating factory service department costs because it represents activity by producing departments.

explanations.A: Salaries of service department employees is not a good allocation basis for anything. The salaries of the service department employees are part of the costs that will be allocated, so they cannot serve as an activity base on which to determine allocations. The activity base used for the allocation of service department costs should represent the usage of the service department services by the user departments.
explanations.B: The activity base used for the allocation of service department costs should represent the usage of the service department services by the user departments. The use of units sold is usually not a good allocation basis for anything except shipping costs or sales related costs.
explanations.D: The amount of materials used does not provide a good basis for allocating factory service department costs. The activity base used for the allocation of service department costs should represent the usage of the service department services by the user departments.

question: Boston Furniture Company manufactures several steel products. It has three production departments, Fabricating, Assembly, and Finishing. The service departments include Maintenance, Material Handling, and Designing. Currently, the company does not allocate service department costs to the production departments. John Baker, who has recently joined the company as the new cost accountant, believes that service department rates should be developed and charged to the production departments for services requested. If the company adopts this new policy, the production department managers would be least likely to

options.A: be encouraged to control costs.
options.B: request an excessive amount of service.
options.C: replace outdated and inefficient systems.
options.D: refrain from using necessary services.

correctExplanation: If the company begins charging service department costs against the production departments for services requested, production department managers would be unlikely to request an excessive amount of service. They would want to keep their costs as low as possible, so they would be more likely to limit their requests for service.

explanations.A: If the company begins charging service department costs against the production departments for services requested, production department managers would be more likely, not less likely, to be encouraged to control costs. They would want to keep their costs as low as possible, so they would want to control costs by limiting their requests for service.
explanations.C: If the company begins charging service department costs against the production departments for services requested, production department managers would be more likely, not less likely, to replace outdated and inefficient systems. By replacing outdated and inefficient systems that require more service with new systems that require little or no service, they would reduce their requests for service and reduce the amount of service costs charged against them.
explanations.D: If the company begins charging service department costs against the production departments for services requested, production department managers would be more likely, not less likely, to refrain from using necessary services. They might not request service when it was needed in order to keep the amount of service costs charged against them as low as possible.

question: Albert Hathaway recently joined Brannen University as the chief information officer of the University Computing Services Department. His assigned task is to help reduce the recurrent problem of cost overruns due to uncontrolled computer usage by the user community, while at the same time not curtailing the use of information technology for research and teaching. To ensure goal congruence, which one of the following algorithms should be used to allocate the cost of the University Computing Services Department to other departments within the university?

options.A: Actual rate times budgeted hours of computer usage.
options.B: Budgeted rate times budgeted hours of computer usage.
options.C: Actual rate times actual hours of computer usage.
options.D: Budgeted rate times actual hours of computer usage.

correctExplanation: So that user departments can know the hourly rate they will be charged in advance, the budgeted hourly rate should be used. To encourage them to limit their computer usage, they should be charged for their actual hours of computer usage.

explanations.A: If the actual rate is used, the user departments will not be able to know in advance what hourly rate they will be charged, because the hourly rate can only be determined after the usage takes place and the costs for it are known. Without adequate information for planning, the user departments will not be able to properly control their usage. Furthermore, charging user departments for their budgeted hours of computer usage will not encourage them to limit their actual usage.
explanations.B: Charging user departments for their budgeted hours of computer usage will not encourage them to limit their actual hours of usage.
explanations.C: If the actual rate is used, the user departments will not be able to know in advance what hourly rate they will be charged, because the hourly rate can only be determined after the usage takes place and the costs for it are known. Without adequate information for planning, the user departments will not be able to properly control their usage.

question: A corporation allocates indirect corporate overhead costs to its operating divisions. The company uses a cause-and-effect criterion in the selection of appropriate allocation bases. Which of the following would be an appropriate allocation base to assign the costs of the corporate personnel department to the operating divisions using a cause-and-effect criterion?

options.A: Total service years of employees in each division.
options.B: Number of employees in each division.
options.C: Total book value of identifiable division assets.
options.D: Square footage of space occupied by each division.

correctExplanation: Presumably the cost driver for the personnel department would be the number of employees, and therefore this is the most cause and effect method of allocating the personnel department costs.

explanations.A: Though the number of service years is a personnel related measure, how long someone has worked would not significantly impact the amount of time the personnel department spends on employees in each division.
explanations.C: Total book value of division assets would not be a cause and effect criteria for the allocation of the personnel department costs.
explanations.D: Square footage of space would not be a cause and effect criteria for the allocation of the personnel department costs.

question: Most firms allocate corporate and other support costs to divisions and departments for all of the following reasons except to

options.A: remind profit center managers that earnings must be adequate to cover some share of the indirect costs.
options.B: create competition between divisions and departments and their managers.
options.C: stimulate profit center managers to put pressure on central managers to control service costs.
options.D: fix accountability and evaluate profit centers.

correctExplanation: This is not a reason to allocate service and support costs to divisions and departments. The managers of the service departments should not be held accountable to the user departments to control their costs but rather to top management.

explanations.A: Internal allocation of support costs is done because if a company calculates its cost of production but does not include the costs of its service departments, it will calculate a cost of production that is less than the actual total cost. As a result of this incorrect calculation, the company’s pricing decisions will not be correct, and in a worst-case scenario, the company may sell the product for less than it actually costs to produce it. Allocating service costs to divisions and departments reminds profit center managers that earnings must be adequate to cover the indirect costs, and allocating service costs provides the needed information to those making pricing decisions.
explanations.B: A spirit of competition can be very motivating and result in achievement of company goals, so this is a reason to allocate corporate and support costs to divisions and departments.
explanations.D: Allocating internal service and support costs to divisions and departments that are profit centers makes it possible to see whether profit centers are generating adequate profits and makes them accountable for their performance.

question: When allocating costs from one department to another, a dual-rate cost-allocation method may be used. The dual-rate cost-allocation method is most useful when

options.B: two or more products are produced.
options.C: two or more cost pools are to be allocated.
options.D: costs are separated into variable-cost and fixed-cost subpools.

correctExplanation: The dual-rate cost-allocation method breaks the cost of each service department into two pools, a variable-cost pool and a fixed-cost pool, and allocates each cost pool using a different cost-allocation base. explanations.C: The dual-rate cost-allocation method is no more useful when two or more cost pools are to be allocated than it is when one cost pool is to be allocated. That is not what "dual" refers to.

Number of employees is the most appropriate allocation base to use to allocate the company’s HR overhead expenses for recruiting, staff training and development, labor law compliance, payroll, record keeping, and employee relations, because the cost driver for those exenses is number of employees in each department. A cost driver is anything--an activity, an event, or a volume of something, for example--that causes costs to be incurred each time the driver occurs. question: Render Inc. has four support departments (maintenance, power, human resources, and legal) and three operating departments. The support departments provide services to the operating departments as well as to the other support departments. The method of allocating the costs of the support departments that best recognizes the mutual services rendered by support departments to other support departments is the

options.A: step-down allocation method.
options.B: reciprocal allocation method.
options.C: dual-rate allocation method.
options.D: direct allocation method.

correctExplanation: The reciprocal method is the only service cost allocation method that recognizes all of the services that are provided by the service departments to the other service departments. Therefore, it is the method that best recognizes the mutual services rendered by support departments to other support department.

explanations.A: The step-down allocation method recognizes some but not all of the mutual services rendered by support departments to other support departments. The reciprocal method is the only service cost allocation method that recognizes all of the services that are provided by the service departments to the other service departments.
explanations.C: The dual-rate allocation method can be used with either the direct method, the step-down method, or the reciprocal method of cost allocations. It simply means that fixed costs and variable costs are allocated separately. There is nothing about the dual-rate method that necessarily either recognizes or does not recognize the mutual services rendered by support departments to other support departments.
explanations.D: The direct allocation method does not recognize the mutual services rendered by support departments to other support departments at all. The reciprocal method is the only service cost allocation method that recognizes all of the services that are provided by the service departments to the other service departments.

question: Adam Corporation manufactures computer tables and has the following budgeted indirect manufacturing cost information for next year. intro: Adam Corporation manufactures computer tables and has the following budgeted indirect manufacturing cost information for next year. Support Departments Operating Departments Maintenance Systems Machining Fabrication Total
tail: If Adam uses the step-down method, beginning with the Maintenance Department, to allocate support department costs to production departments, the total overhead (rounded to the nearest dollar) for the Machining Department to allocate to its products would be
correctExplanation: In the step-down method, the costs of one of the service departments are allocated first, and those costs are allocated to the other service department(s) and the production departments. When the second service department’s costs are allocated, the second service department's costs to be allocated include its own costs incurred plus the costs allocated to it from the first service department. Those costs are allocated to the other service departments except for the first service department and to the production departments. Any service department whose costs have already been allocated does not receive an allocation from any other service department. Beginning with the Maintenance Department, the first amount to be allocated is $360,000 in budgeted overhead for Maintenance. That is allocated 10% or $36,000 to Systems, the other service department; 50% or $180,000 to Machining, and 40% or $144,000 to Fabrication. The next department’s costs to be allocated is Systems. The Systems costs to be allocated include the Systems Department’s budgeted overhead of $95,000 plus the amount allocated to Systems from Maintenance, which is $36,000, for a total of $131,000 to be allocated. In allocating the Systems costs, we do not allocate any cost to the Maintenance Department, which is budgeted to use 5% of the Systems Department’s services. That leaves the Machining and the Fabrication departments to receive the Systems Department’s cost allocations. The Machining Department is budgeted to receive 45% of the Systems Department’s services, and the Fabrication Department is budgeted to receive 50%. But instead of multiplying the total to be allocated ($131,000) by 45% to get the amount of Systems cost to allocate to Machining, we need to remember that the users’ usage totals only 95% because nothing is to be allocated to Maintenance. Therefore, the factor to use in allocating the Systems Department’s costs to Machining is 0.45/0.95, which equals 0.473684. The Systems Department’s cost allocated to Machining will be $131,000 × 0.473684, which equals $62,053. In addition to the Systems Department’s allocated costs of $62,053, the Machining Department will be allocated the $180,000 from Maintenance, and it will have budgeted overhead in its own department of $200,000. Thus, the total overhead for the Machining Department to allocate to its products is $200,000 of its own overhead + $180,000 from Maintenance + $62,053 from Systems, which equals $442,053.

explanations.A: In the step-down method, the costs of one of the service departments are allocated first, and those costs are allocated to the other service department(s) and the production departments. When the second service department’s costs are allocated, the second service department's costs to be allocated include its own costs incurred plus the costs allocated to it from the first service department. Those costs are allocated to the other service departments except for the first service department and to the production departments. Any service department whose costs have already been allocated does not receive an allocation from any other service department. This answer results from allocating 45% of the System's Department's budgeted overhead costs of $95,000, or $42,750, to the Machining Department. This is incorrect for two reasons. One, the Systems Department's costs to be allocated should include not only its own budgeted overhead of $95,000 but also the costs allocated to it from Maintenance, which are $36,000, for a total of $131,000 to be allocated by the Systems Department. Second, remember that in allocating the Systems costs, we do not allocate any cost to the Maintenance Department, even though Maintenance is budgeted to use 5% of the Systems Department's services. That leaves only the Machining and the Fabrication departments to receive the Systems Department’s cost allocations; and the amounts allocated to those two departments need to total to 100%, not 95%, of the total Systems costs of $131,000. The Machining Department is budgeted to receive 45% of the Systems Department’s services, and the Fabrication Department is budgeted to receive 50%. But instead of multiplying the total to be allocated ($131,000) by 45% to get the amount of Systems cost to allocate to Machining, we need to remember that the users’ usage totals only 95% because nothing is to be allocated to Maintenance. Therefore, the factor to use in allocating the Systems Department’s costs to Machining is 0.45/0.95, which equals 0.473684. The Systems Department’s cost allocated to Machining will be $131,000 × 0.473684, which equals $62,053.
explanations.C: This is the total overhead for the Machining Department to allocate to its products using the direct method. The question says to use the step-down method, beginning with the Systems Department's costs.
explanations.D: This answer results partially from allocating the Systems Department's costs first. The question says to begin with the Maintenance Department. However, another mistake is allocating the Maintenance Department's costs to the Machining Department using the budgeted usage for the Systems Department, instead of the budgeted usage for the Maintenance Department.

question: Wilcox Industrial has two support departments, the Information Systems Department and the Personnel Department, and two manufacturing departments, the Machining Department and the Assembly Department. question: Wilcox Industrial has two support departments, the Information Systems Department and the Personnel Department, and two manufacturing departments, the Machining Department and the Assembly Department. The support departments service each other as well as the two production departments. Company studies have shown that the Personnel Department provides support to a greater number of departments than the Information Systems Department. If Wilcox uses the step-down method of departmental allocation, which one of the following cost allocations would not occur? Some of the costs of the

options.A: Personnel Department would be allocated to the Assembly Department.
options.B: Personnel Department would be allocated to the Information Systems Department.
options.C: Personnel Department would be allocated to the Assembly Department and the Machining Department.
options.D: Information Systems Department would be allocated to the Personnel Department.

correctExplanation: In order to use the step-down method, there must be an order in which we allocate the costs of the service departments. A popular method is to determine the order according to the percentage of each department’s services that are provided to other service departments. The department that provides the highest percentage of its services to other service departments is allocated first. Then the department that provides the next highest percentage of its services to other service departments comes next, and so on. The first service department will have its costs allocated to the other service departments and the production departments. The second service department’s costs (which now include its share of the first service department’s costs) will be allocated to the other service departments (but not to the first service department that has already been allocated) and the production departments. Once a service department has had its costs allocated, no costs will be allocated from other service departments to it. The question tells us that company studies have shown that the Personnel Department provides support to a greater number of departments than the Information Systems Department does. Therefore, we will assume that the Personnel Department's costs will be allocated first, and some of the Personnel Department's costs will be allocated to the Information Systems Department. The Information Systems Department's costs, including its allocation of Personnel Department costs, are then allocated to the production departments, but not to the Personnel Department. Thus, under the step-down method, none of the costs of the Information Systems Department would be allocated to the Personnel Department.

The department that provides the highest percentage of its services to other service departments is allocated first. Then the department that provides the next highest percentage of its services to other service departments comes next, and so on. The first service department will have its costs allocated to the other service departments and the production departments. The second service department’s costs (which now include its share of the first service department’s costs) will be allocated to the other service departments (but not to the first service department that has already been allocated) and the production departments. Once a service department has had its costs allocated, no costs will be allocated from other service departments to it. question: The method for allocating service department costs that best recognizes the mutual services rendered to other service departments is the

options.A: Dual-rate allocation method.
options.B: Step-down allocation method.
options.C: Reciprocal allocation method.
options.D: Direct allocation method.

correctExplanation: The reciprocal allocation method recognizes reciprocity among service department by explicitly including the mutual services rendered among support departments.

explanations.A: The three methods of allocating shared-service department costs when an organization has several shared service departments and the shared service departments provide support not only to the operating departments but to the other shared service departments as well are: The direct method The step (or step-down) method The reciprocal method The dual-rate method breaks the cost of each service department into two pools, a variable-cost pool and a fixed-cost pool, and each cost pool is allocated separately using a different cost allocation base. If a company has shared-service departments that provide services to each other, the company may use either the single-rate method, in which all the service department costs are put into one cost pool and the costs are allocated using one allocation base; or the dual-rate method, in which fixed costs and variable costs are allocated separately. If the dual-rate method is used, the company simply does two separate cost allocations, one to allocate the fixed costs and one to allocate the variable costs. The company may use any method of shared-service cost allocation for the separate allocations: the direct method, the step-down method, or the reciprocal method. But "dual rate" and "single rate" are not methods of allocation. They simply describe whether fixed and variable costs are allocated separately or whether they are all allocated together in one single allocation. Please see the correct answer explanaation for more information.
explanations.B: The step-down allocation method allocates service department costs to other service departments and production departments usually starting with the service department that provides the most service to other service departments. This method allows for partial recognition of reciprocity of services among service departments. Please see the correct answer explanaation for more information.
explanations.D: The direct allocation method allocates the cost of service departments directly to the production departments without any intermediate allocations to other service departments. Thus, this method does not recognize any reciprocity of services among service departments. Please see the correct answer explanaation for more information.

question: Cotton Company has two service departments and three operating departments. In allocating service department costs to the operating departments, which of the following three methods (direct, step-down, reciprocal) will result in the same amount of service department costs being allocated to each operating department, regardless of the order in which the service department costs are allocated?

options.A: Direct method only.
options.B: Direct and step-down methods only.
options.C: Step-down and reciprocal methods only.

correctExplanation: There are three methods of allocating service costs: direct, step-down and reciprocal. This question is asking: if in doing service cost allocation, you change which department you allocate costs to first, under which of the three methods would the amount allocated to each department not be changed? The only method where the result is affected by which department is allocated costs first is the step-down method. In the step-down method, the amount allocated to each department depends on which department is allocated costs first and thus the allocation changes if the department allocated costs first changes. Thus, if the allocation is being done using either the direct or the reciprocal method, the amounts allocated to each department would not be affected by which department receives the first allocation.

correctExplanation: Department S1's costs to allocate = 27,000 + 0.20 S2 Department S2's costs to allocate = 18,000 + 0.10 S1 S2 = 18,000 + 0.10(27,000 + 0.20 S2) S2 = 18,000 + 2700 + 0.02 S2 S2 = 20,700 + 0.02 S2 0.98 S2 = 20,700 S2 = 21,122.45 S1 = 27,000 + 0.20(21,122.45) S1 = 31,224.49 Department P2 used 40% of Department S1's services, so the cost allocated to Department P2 from Department S1 is 31,224.49 × 0.40 = $12,489.80. The IT department allocates its overhead based on the number of computers and Engineering allocates its overhead based on square footage. The company uses the reciprocal allocation method. tail: How much of IT’s overhead should be allocated to the F&B department?
correctExplanation: The reciprocal method recognizes all of the services provided by the shared service departments to the other shared service departments. It is calculated using multiple equations, as many as there are service departments. IT costs to allocate = IT costs + IT's percentage of Engineering's costs. IT is responsible for 5% of Engineering's costs because IT occupies 500 square feet of the total 10,000 square feet. Let IT stand for the IT department's costs and EN stand for the Engineering department's costs: IT's total costs to allocate = 100,000 + 0.05 EN Engineering's costs to allocate = Engineering's costs + Engineering's percentage of IT's costs. Engineering is responsible for 10% of IT's costs because Engineering uses 10 computers of the total 100 computers that IT supports. EN's total costs to allocate = 200,000 + 0.10 IT Solve for IT's total costs to allocate by substituting the right side of the equation that expresses EN's total costs to allocate into the "EN" in the equation representing IT's total costs to allocate: IT = 100,000 + (0.05[200,000 + 0.10 IT]) IT = 100,000 + 10,000 + 0.005 IT IT = 110,000 + 0.005 IT 0.995 IT = 110,000 IT cost to allocate = 110,552.76 The F & B department uses 50% of IT's services because it has 50 computers out of the total 100 computers. Therefore, 50% of IT's costs to allocate are allocated to the F & B department: $110,552.76 x 0.50 = $55,276.38.

explanations.B: This is 20% of $100,000. This is not the amount of IT's overhead to be allocated to the F & B department using the reciprocal method. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: A large company is in the process of allocating service department costs to revenue-generating departments. Under which one of the following allocation methods will the amount allocated to each revenue-generating department be different if the order in which service department costs are allocated is different?

options.A: Direct method.
options.B: Step-down method.
options.C: Activity-based method.
options.D: Reciprocal method.

correctExplanation: Under the step-down method, the amount of expense allocated to each operating department will be different if the order in which service department costs are allocated is changed. When the step-down method of shared service allocation is used with multiple shared service departments that provide services to each other, the first shared service department’s costs are allocated to the other shared service departments and the operating departments. The second shared service department’s costs (which now include its share of the first shared service department’s costs) are allocated next to the other shared service departments (but not to the first shared service department that has already been allocated) and the operating departments. Once a shared service department’s costs have been allocated, no costs will be allocated to it from other shared service departments.

explanations.A: Under the direct method, the amount of expense allocated to each operating department will not be different if the order in which the service department costs are allocated is changed. When the direct method of shared service allocation is used, the services provided by the different shared service departments to each other are ignored. The company simply allocates all the shared service departments’ costs directly to the operating departments on a basis that is reasonable and equitable to the operating departments for each service department. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: Activity-based costing (ABC) is a method of allocating overhead costs to cost objects (usually products, services, or customers) based on cost drivers. It is not a method of allocating service department costs to revenue-generating departments. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: Under the reciprocal method, the amount of expense allocated to each operating department will not be different if the order in which the service department costs are allocated is changed. The reciprocal method recognizes all of the services provided by the shared service departments to all the other shared service departments. The shared service departments each allocate some of their costs to the other shared service departments. As a result, the total amount allocated by each shared service department will be greater than its own overhead costs, since each shared service department must allocate all of its own costs plus some of the other shared service departments’ costs that have been allocated to it. The reciprocal method uses simultaneous, or multiple, equations to do the allocations. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

intro: Fabricating and Finishing are the two production departments of a manufacturing company. Building Operations and Information Services are service departments that provide support to the two production departments as well as to each other. The company employs departmental overhead rates in the two production departments to allocate the service department costs to the production departments. Square footage is used to allocate building operations, and computer time is used to allocate information services. The costs of the service departments and relevant operating data for the departments are as follows: Building Operations Information Services Fabricating Finishing Costs:
tail: If the company employs the step method to allocate the costs of the service departments and if information services costs are allocated first, then the total amount of service department costs (Information Services and Building Operations) allocated to finishing would be:
correctExplanation: Under the step method we will first allocate the costs of the information services department to all of the other departments (including building operations) and then we will allocate the building operations costs (their own costs plus their share of the information services costs) to the production departments. The information services costs are $1,200,000 and the usage of their services totaled 2,000 computer hours. Of the total information services costs, 10% ($120,000) will be allocated to building operations, 60% ($720,000) will be allocated to the fabricating department, and 30% ($360,000) will be allocated to the finishing department. The allocation of information services costs means that there is now $670,000 of costs in the building operations department that need to be allocated to the production departments (its own $550,000 plus the $120,000 allocated to it from information services). The building operations costs totaling $670,000 will be allocated to the fabricating and finishing departments only. Information services will not be included in the allocation of the building operations costs, since information services' costs have already been allocated out. So the allocation base for the building operations costs is 16,000 square feet used by fabricating and 24,000 square feet used by finishing, for a total of 40,000 square feet. The finishing department occupies 60% of the total 40,000 square feet (24,000 ÷ 40,000). The share of the building operations costs that is allocated to the finishing department is therefore $402,000 ($670,000 × 0.60). This is added to the $360,000 that was allocated to the finishing department from the information services department, giving a total of $762,000 allocated to the finishing department.

explanations.B: This answer uses the direct method to allocate the costs of both departments.
explanations.C: This answer is a result of two mistakes: (1) allocating the Building Operations costs first instead of allocating the Information Services' costs first when the problem says to allocate the Building Operations costs first; and (2) allocating some of the Information Services' costs to Building Operations in the second allocation. In the step method, once a service department's costs have been allocated to other departments, no other service departments' costs can be allocated to that service department.
explanations.D: This answer allocates some of the building operations costs to the information services department. In the step method, once a service department's costs have been allocated to other departments, no other service departments' costs can be allocated to that service department.

correctExplanation: Under the direct method of service cost allocation, we ignore the services that are provided from one service department to another. explanations.C: This answer included the allocation of the power department costs to the maintenance department as well as the production departments. Under the direct method, service department costs are not allocated to the other service departments.

question: There are several methods for allocating service department costs to the production departments. The method that recognizes service provided by one service department to another but does not recognize reciprocal interdepartmental service is the:

options.A: Reciprocal method.
options.B: Step-down method.
options.C: Variable method.
options.D: Direct method.

correctExplanation: Under the step method, the services that one department provides to the other departments are recognized. In the allocation of the costs of the third service department, no costs are allocated back to the first or second service department, and so on.

explanations.A: Under the reciprocal method the costs of the service departments are allocated to each other, so there is a recognition of reciprocal interdepartmental service.
explanations.C: This answer is incorrect because it is not a method of allocating service department costs.

In order to allocate the costs of the quality control department to assembly, we need to determine what percentage of the quality control time that was used by the production departments was used by assembly. intro: The managers of Rochester Manufacturing are discussing ways to allocate the cost of service departments such as Quality Control and Maintenance to the production departments. To aid them in this discussion, the controller has provided the following information: Quality Control Maintenance Machining Assembly Total
tail: If Rochester Manufacturing uses the reciprocal method of allocating service costs, the total amount of quality control costs (rounded to the nearest dollar) to be allocated to the other departments would be:
correctExplanation: The reciprocal method requires the use of two formulas. The two formulas are based on the total costs budgeted to be incurred by each service department and the budgeted percentage of each service department's usage of the other service department's total services provided. The Quality Control department's total budgeted costs (QC) equal its own $350,000 in costs plus 25% of the Maintenance department's costs. The 25% is calculated as 10,000 budgeted hours of maintenance usage for the Quality Control department divided by the 40,000 total budgeted hours of maintenance usage for the whole company. Therefore, the equation for the Quality Control department's total costs is QC = $350,000 + 0.25M. The Maintenance department's total budgeted costs (M) equal its own $200,000 in costs plus 20% of the Quality Control department's costs. The 20% is calculated as 7,000 budgeted hours of quality control usage for the Maintenance department divided by the 35,000 total budgeted hours of quality control usage for the whole company. Therefore, the equation for the Maintenance department's total costs is M = $200,000 + 0.20QC. Now, we can solve this for either variable by substituting one equation into the other. We will solve for QC (because this is what the question asks for), as follows: QC = $350,000 + 0.25($200,000 + 0.20QC) QC = $350,000 + $50,000 + 0.05QC 0.95QC = $400,000 QC = $421,053. This is the amount of costs that the QC department must allocate to the two production departments and the maintenance department.

explanations.A: This is the total amount of overhead costs budgeted to be incurred by the Quality Control department. However, it is not the total amount of Quality Control costs to be allocated. When the reciprocal method of allocating service costs is used, each service department's costs to be allocated include not only their own incurred costs but also a portion of the other service department costs, based on their usage of the other service departments' services.
explanations.B: The question asks for the total amount of quality control costs to be allocated to the other departments. "Other departments" means the two production departments and the maintenance department. This answer is the amount of the quality control costs that will be allocated to the two production departments. It does not include the amount that will be allocated to the maintenance department. It is not necessary to calculate the actual departmental allocations in order to answer this question. Once you have calculated the total amount of quality control costs to be allocated, you have the answer to the question.
explanations.D: This is the total amount of maintenance department costs to be allocated to the other departments. The question asks for the total amount of quality control costs to be allocated to the other departments.

question: Logo Inc. has two data services departments (the Systems Department and the Facilities Department) that provide support to the company’s three production departments (Machining Department, Assembly Department, and Finishing Department). The overhead costs of the Systems Department are allocated to other departments on the basis of computer usage hours. Department Overhead Computer Usage Hours Square Feet Occupied Systems $200,000 300 1,000 Facilities 100,000 900 600 Machining 400,000 3,600 2,000 Assembly 550,000 1,800 3,000 Finishing 620,000 2,700 5,000 9,300 11,600 Logo employs the step-down method of allocating service department costs and begins with the Systems Department. Which one of the following correctly denotes the amount of the Systems Department's overhead that would be allocated to the Facilities Department and the Facilities Department's overhead charges that would be allocated to the Machining Department?

The overhead costs of the Facilities Department are allocated based on square feet occupied (in thousands). Other information pertaining to Logo is as follows. tail: Logo employs the step-down method of allocating service department costs and begins with the Systems Department. Which one of the following correctly denotes the amount of the Systems Department's overhead that would be allocated to the Facilities Department and the Facilities Department's overhead charges that would be allocated to the Machining Department?

options.A: $20,000 would be allocated from Systems to Facilities; $24,000 would be allocated from Facilities to Machining.
options.B: $19,355 would be allocated from Systems to Facilities; $20,578 would be allocated from Facilities to Machining.
options.C: $20,000 would be allocated from Systems to Facilities; $20,000 would be allocated from Facilities to Machining.
options.D: $0 would be allocated from Systems to Facilities; $20,000 would be allocated from Facilities to Machining.

correctExplanation: In the step-down method, the costs of one of the service departments are allocated first, and those costs are allocated to the other service department(s) and the production departments. When the second service department’s costs are allocated, those costs are allocated to any service department(s) other than the first service department allocated and to the production departments. Any service department whose costs have already been allocated does not receive an allocation from any other service department. Beginning with the Systems Department, its overhead cost of $200,000 is allocated to the Facilities, Machining, Assembly and Finishing departments on the basis of their computer usage hours. The usage of those four departments totals 900 + 3,600 + 1,800 + 2,700 = 9,000 hours. The usage of the Facilities Department is 900 hours, or 10% of that. Thus, the Facilities Department is allocated 10% of the Systems Department’s overhead cost of $200,000, or $20,000. The Facilities Department has overhead cost to allocate of $100,000 plus the $20,000 allocated to it from Systems, for a total of $120,000. Facilities costs are allocated on the basis of square feet occupied by the Machining, Assembly and Finishing departments. The square feet occupied by those three departments totals 2,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 = 10,000 square feet. The square feet occupied by the Machining Department is 2,000 square feet, or 20% of that. Thus, the Machining Department is allocated 20% of the Facilities Department’s overhead cost of $120,000, or $24,000.

explanations.B: This answer results from calculating the cost allocations by dividing each individual department's usage of the allocation base by the total usage by all the departments (9,300 computer usage hours or 11,600 square feet occupied). The proration of the costs should be based not on the total usage by all departments but on the total usage by only the departments to which the costs are being allocated.
explanations.C: This answer results from failing to include in the Facilities cost to be allocated the cost allocated to Facilities from Systems. The amount of Facilities cost to be allocated should be its own $100,000 in costs plus the amount of Systems Department cost allocated to Facilities.
explanations.D: This answer results from beginning the allocations with the Facilities Department and also from not allocating any costs of the Facilities Department to the Systems Department, as would be appropriate if the allocation began with Facilities. But the question says to begin with the Systems Department, not with the Facilities Department.

So the total overhead of the Systems department, which is $200,000, will be allocated by dividing that amount by 8,100 to calculate the allocation rate per hour used by the production departments.

explanations.A: 9,000 hours is the total of computer usage hours for all of the departments other than the Systems department. The Systems costs will be allocated only to the production departments. So the divisor used in calculating the allocation rate should be the total of the production departments' usage hours.
explanations.B: 1,200 hours is the total of computer usage hours for the Systems and Facilities departments. The Systems costs will be allocated only to the production departments. So the divisor used in calculating the allocation rate should be the total of the production departments' usage hours.
explanations.C: 9,300 hours is the total of computer usage hours for all of the departments, including the Systems department. The Systems costs will be allocated only to the production departments. So the divisor used in calculating the allocation rate should be the total of the production departments' usage hours. Supply Chain Management(4)

question: Which of the following statements best describes the function and layout of manufacturing cells in lean production?

options.A: Manufacturing cells require each worker to specialize in a single task to ensure high quality and efficiency.
options.B: Manufacturing cells aim to minimize downtime by enabling workers to operate any machine within the cell and reducing unnecessary movements.
options.C: Manufacturing cells are organized to maximize the distance materials travel between processes.
options.D: Manufacturing cells are designed to handle large batch production efficiently by using centralized workstations.

correctExplanation: Manufacturing cells are designed to reduce downtime and waste by ensuring workers are cross-trained to operate all machines within the cell. This flexibility allows for smoother operation and quicker response to any issues that arise, reducing downtime and unnecessary movements.

explanations.A: In manufacturing cells, workers are cross-trained to perform multiple tasks, which helps in maintaining continuous flow and adaptability. Specializing in a single task can lead to inefficiencies and bottlenecks, contrary to the principles of lean production.
explanations.C: The goal of manufacturing cells is to minimize the distance materials travel between processes to reduce wasted motion and improve efficiency, not maximize it. The manufacturing cells are arranged to streamline the flow of products through each necessary process with minimal movement.
explanations.D: Lean production emphasizes continuous flow and smaller batches, not large batch production. Manufacturing cells support this by enabling flexible and efficient small-batch or continuous production rather than centralized workstations for large batches.

question: Which of the following is considered a wasteful activity addressed by lean production?

options.A: Maintaining a detailed inventory of all raw materials.
options.B: Implementing a robust quality control process.
options.C: Conducting thorough market research to understand customer needs.
options.D: Overproduction of items that cannot be sold.

correctExplanation: Overproduction is a classic form of waste in lean production. Producing more items than needed leads to excess inventory, increased storage costs, and potential obsolescence, all of which are considered wasteful.

explanations.A: While managing inventory is important for lean production, maintaining a detailed inventory itself is not considered wasteful. However, having excessive inventory beyond what is needed is considered wasteful. Lean production aims to optimize inventory levels to reduce waste.
explanations.B: Quality control processes are essential to ensuring that products meet customer expectations and reduce defects. This is not considered wasteful but rather a necessary practice to maintain high standards and avoid the costs associated with rework or returns.
explanations.C: Market research helps in understanding customer requirements and aligning production with demand. This is not a wasteful activity but a strategic one that helps in reducing waste by preventing the production of unwanted goods. Just-In-Time Systems and MRP, MRPII, ERP(12)

topic: Just-In-Time Systems and MRP, MRPII, ERP
question: All of the following are benefits of just-in-time manufacturing except that it

options.A: can significantly reduce inventory.
options.B: helps eliminate rework costs.
options.C: helps produce a higher-quality product in less time.
options.D: allows for minor defects without shutting down operations.

correctExplanation: Just-in-time inventory and manufacturing systems do not allow for minor defects. It is just the opposite. Having a just-in-time system requires elimination of defects and also improves workers' ability to eliminate defects. Because of the close coordination between and among workstations and the minimum inventories held at each workstation when JIT is in use, defects caused at one workstation very quickly affect other workstations. Therefore, JIT requires problems and defects to be solved by eliminating their root causes as quickly as possible. Workers need to be able to trace problems to their source and resolve them at the point where they originated.

explanations.A: This is a true statement. The goal of a JIT system is to minimize the level of inventories held in the plant at all stages of production, including raw materials, work-in-process, and finished goods inventories while meeting customer demand in a timely manner with high-quality products at the lowest possible cost. The main idea of JIT is that nothing is produced until the next process in the assembly line needs it. In other words, nothing is produced until a customer orders it, and then it is produced very quickly. This "demand-pull" feature of JIT requires close coordination between and among workstations. Close coordination between and among workstations can keep the flow of goods smooth in spite of the low levels of inventory. An important advantage of a JIT system is reduction in the cost of carrying the inventory. In addition to reducing the amount invested in the inventory, the cost savings include reduction in the risk of damage, theft, loss, or a lack of ability to sell the finished goods.
explanations.B: This is a true statement. Having a just-in-time system requires elimination of defects and also improves workers' ability to eliminate defects. Because defects are eliminated, rework costs can also be eliminated. Please see the correct answer for more information.
explanations.C: This is a true statement. Just-in-time inventory and manufacturing systems help in meeting customer demand in a timely manner with high-quality products at the lowest possible cost. Please see the correct answer for more information.

topic: Just-In-Time Systems and MRP, MRPII, ERP
question: Presario Inc. recently installed just-in-time production and purchasing systems. If Presario’s experience is similar to that of other companies, Presario will likely

options.A: increase its dollar investment in finished goods inventory.
options.B: reduce the number of suppliers with which it does business.
options.C: increase the size of individual orders of raw materials.
options.D: be less reliant on sales orders as a "trigger" mechanism for production runs.

correctExplanation: With a JIT system a company works with a few suppliers very closely to ensure the quality of materials as well as the timing of many smaller shipments.

explanations.A: JIT systems produce goods as they are needed. Utilizing a JIT system would reduce the size of the finished goods inventory, as items theoretically go directly from finished production to sales.
explanations.C: JIT relies on receiving many smaller shipments of raw materials rather than on large orders. Large orders increase inventory costs as well as storage and handling expenses.
explanations.D: The main idea of JIT is that nothing is produced until the next process in the assembly line needs it. Therefore, JIT is a "pull system" rather than a "push system." Nothing is produced until it is needed, so essentially nothing is produced until a customer orders it. Therefore, JIT is actually more reliant on sales orders as a trigger for production runs, not less.

question: All of the following statements are true about Kanban except

options.A: Kanban is a part of a JIT system and its purpose is to manage the flow on a manufacturing assembly line.
options.B: The supplier delivers components to the production line on an "as needed" basis, signaled by receipt of a card and empty container, eliminating storage in the production area.
options.C: Kanban was originally developed at Toyota.
options.D: "Kanban" is a Japanese term meaning "continuous improvement."

correctExplanation: Kanban is a Japanese term for "visual record." It is a simple parts movement system or an inventory system in which 'cards' or 'tickets' are used to keep track of inventory and its movement. The term "kaizen" is the Japanese term for "continuous improvement."

explanations.A: Kanban is part of a JIT system and its purpose is to manage the flow on a manufacturing assembly line. This is a chain process where orders flow from one process to another, so production of components is pulled to the production line, rather than the pushed (as is done in the traditional forecast-oriented system).
explanations.B: Kanban is a simple parts movement system or an inventory system in which 'cards' or 'tickets' are used to keep track of inventory and its movement. The supplier delivers components to the production line on an "as needed" basis, signaled by receipt of a card and empty container, eliminating storage in the production area.
explanations.C: Kanban was developed at Toyota.

topic: Just-In-Time Systems and MRP, MRPII, ERP
question: In a just-in-time-inventory (JIT) system, which statement is false:

options.A: JIT is a pull system.
options.B: JIT combines purchasing, production and inventory control into one function.
options.C: The main idea in a JIT system is that the company does not produce anything until the next process requires it.
options.D: Because JIT is a push system, production is not driven by the expected demand for the product.

correctExplanation: The main idea of JIT is that nothing is produced until the next process in the assembly line needs it. JIT is a "pull system" rather than a "push system." In a push system, a department produces and sends all that it can to the next step for further processing, which means that the manufacturer is producing something without understanding consumer demand. This can result in large, useless stocks of inventory. Because the idea of JIT is that nothing will be produced until the next process needs it, technically this means that nothing will be produced until a customer orders it. However, this may not actually be possible in some industries, so in those industries, production is driven by the expected demand for the product.

explanations.A: This is a true statement. JIT is a pull system, which is based on a manufacturing philosophy that combines purchasing, production and inventory control into one function. This reduces the level of inventory that is held within the company at all stages of production, and lowers the cost of carrying the inventory.
explanations.B: This is a true statement.
explanations.C: This is a true statement.

question: Urban Blooms is a company that grows flowering plants and sells them in attractively designed container arrangements to upscale hotels, restaurants and offices throughout the greater New York City metropolitan area. The only exception was importing expensive, large containers from Mexico. After five years in business, Urban Blooms had become very profitable and increased its staff from 10 to 200 employees, including horticulturalists, production/design workers, business managers, and sales staff. However, the owners found it increasingly difficult to keep up with the complexities and demands brought about by the company’s continuing growth. It became apparent that several areas of the business were not time- or cost-effective for Urban Blooms, such as mixing its own potting soil for the plants and maintaining payroll accounting. Urban Blooms contacted Hampshire Farms to create a special potting soil mix for its plants and hired Lindeman Associates to handle the company’s payroll accounting requirements. This process is referred to as:

options.A: Activity-based costing (ABC).
options.B: Materials resource planning (MRP).
options.C: Outsourcing.
options.D: Lean production.

correctExplanation: A company outsources a particular function or functions to an outside specialist to free up its own resources, allowing the company to focus on its primary operations. explanations.A: The process outlined is not ABC.
